book.title: An Inspector Calls: The Complete Text Guide
book.subject: English Literature

units.title: How you are examined on this play
units.summary: Every board asks for an argument about Priestley’s choices, but the marks are split differently. Check what your board rewards before you plan.

questions.prompt: On the Pearson Edexcel paper, which assessment objective carries no marks on the An Inspector Calls question?
questions.explanation: Edexcel gives 16 marks to AO1, 16 to AO3 and 8 to AO4, so AO2 has none. You still explain how the play works, but as part of your argument.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the exam is true or false.

statements.s: The exam is closed book, so you cannot take the play in with you.
AQA prints an extract from the play for you to start from.
OCR’s question has 2 parts worth 20 marks each.
Eduqas gives marks for context (AO3).

questions.explanation: AQA has no extract: you choose 1 essay from 2. Eduqas does not assess context in this section, while OCR splits its question into (a) and (b).

questions.prompt: Match each board to the feature of its An Inspector Calls question.
pairs: 1 essay from a choice of 2, with no extract
Each question opens with a short quotation from the play
Compare a play extract with an unseen modern drama extract
1 question on the whole play, starting from a printed extract
questions.explanation: These are the formats summarised on page 3 of the guide. Knowing your own format tells you whether to start from an extract, a quotation or nothing at all.

questions.prompt: You cannot remember a quotation word for word. What does every board accept instead?
options: A clear reference to the moment in the play
Nothing: only exact quotations are credited
A quotation from a revision guide
A summary of the whole act
questions.explanation: References need not be word-for-word. Saying exactly where and what happens, such as Eric’s entrance at the end of Act 2, counts as evidence.
questions.misconception: Believing that only perfect quotations earn credit.

questions.prompt: On AQA, how many marks does context (AO3) carry out of the 30 for the essay?
questions.explanation: AQA gives AO1 and AO2 12 marks each and AO3 6. That is why close analysis matters so much on AQA.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true for every board?
options: You must know the whole play, not just one moment.
A clear argument about Priestley’s choices is rewarded more than retelling.
Context is worth the same number of marks on every board.
AO4 is marked on every board’s question.
questions.explanation: Context ranges from 16 marks (Edexcel) to none (Eduqas), and OCR does not mark AO4 on this section. The other 2 statements hold everywhere.

questions.prompt: A student sitting Eduqas plans to open with a paragraph on the 1912 class system before mentioning the extract. What is the best advice?
options: Cut the history paragraph: context earns no marks here, so start with the extract.
Keep it: context is half the marks on every board.
Move it to the end, where context is always rewarded.
Replace it with a paragraph about Priestley’s childhood.
questions.explanation: Eduqas does not assess AO3 on this question, so a history paragraph takes time from analysis. Mention Priestley’s intentions only where they explain a method.
questions.misconception: Assuming every board rewards context in the same way.

questions.prompt: Which board would reward a paragraph of close analysis of the Inspector’s language most, compared with the others?
options: AQA, where AO2 carries 12 of the 30 marks
Pearson Edexcel, where AO2 carries no marks
Neither, because language analysis is never rewarded
questions.explanation: The same paragraph scores well on AQA and Eduqas but earns nothing extra for AO2 on Edexcel, where context carries 16 marks.

questions.prompt: Your friend sits Pearson Edexcel and you sit AQA. Explain 2 ways your answers on the same question should be built differently.
questions.model: Model paragraph: On Edexcel, context is 16 of the 40 marks, so my friend should weave short, specific points about 1912 and 1945 through every paragraph, such as the lack of a welfare state when Mrs Birling refuses Eva. On AQA, context is only 6 of the 30 marks, while language, form and structure carry 12, so I should spend more of each paragraph on Priestley’s methods, such as the dramatic irony of Birling’s predictions. We both need a clear argument, but Edexcel also opens with a quotation, which my friend should use as a way into the whole play rather than the only focus.
checklist: States the different weight of context (16 of 40 against 6 of 30)
Notes that Edexcel gives no marks for AO2 while AQA gives 12
Mentions the Edexcel opening quotation and how to use it
Gives a concrete example from the play for at least 1 point
questions.explanation: A strong answer turns the mark split into a decision about what goes into each paragraph.

questions.prompt: An OCR candidate writes about Eric’s confession in Act 3 in part (a), although the printed extract is from Act 1. Why does this earn little?
options: Part (a) asks you to compare the 2 printed extracts only; other moments belong in part (b).
OCR does not allow any references to Act 3.
Eric is not a main character.
Part (a) is marked only for spelling.
questions.explanation: OCR tells candidates to focus on the 2 extracts in part (a). Wider knowledge of the play is saved for part (b), where you explore another moment.
questions.misconception: Bringing the rest of the play into OCR part (a).

units.title: J.B. Priestley: soldier, writer, broadcaster
units.summary: Priestley grew up in industrial Bradford and fought in the First World War. His socialist beliefs, voiced on BBC radio in 1940, shape the Inspector’s message.

questions.prompt: Where was J.B. Priestley born?
questions.explanation: He was born in Bradford in 1894. Brumley is the fictional town where the play is set.
questions.misconception: Confusing Priestley’s real home town with the play’s fictional setting.

questions.prompt: What was the name of Priestley’s 1940 series of BBC radio talks?
questions.explanation: The talks were called Postscripts and were broadcast on Sunday evenings after the 9 o’clock news.

questions.prompt: Put these events in Priestley’s life in order, earliest first.
items: Born in Bradford
Volunteers for the army
Gives the Postscripts radio talks
Helps to found the Common Wealth party
Writes An Inspector Calls
questions.explanation: Born 1894; volunteered September 1914; Postscripts 1940; Common Wealth 1942; the play was written at the end of the war, usually dated 1944 to 1945.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Priestley worked as a junior clerk in the Bradford wool trade.
He served in the infantry and was badly wounded.
He was too young to fight in the First World War.
He helped to found a socialist party called Common Wealth.

questions.explanation: He volunteered in September 1914, weeks after war began. His work in the wool trade and his war service both feed into the play.

questions.prompt: Which detail from Priestley’s life links most directly to Birling’s confident claim that there will be no war?
options: He had fought in the First World War himself.
questions.explanation: A writer who fought in the war gives Birling a prediction the audience knows is disastrously wrong. That is purpose, not just biography.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Churchill had Priestley taken off the radio because of his politics.’ What is the problem?
options: Historians disagree about why the talks ended, so it should not be stated as fact.
Priestley never broadcast on the radio.
There is no problem: this is a proven fact.
questions.explanation: Accounts differ about why the 1940 series ended. The guide advises leaving it out, because the play does not need it.
questions.misconception: Stating a disputed claim about the radio talks as fact.

questions.prompt: Match each part of Priestley’s life to where it shows in the play.
pairs: Work in the Bradford wool trade
Factories and shops that dismiss workers easily
Service in the First World War
Birling’s mistaken certainty that war will not come
A final speech that seems addressed to the audience
The idea that people share responsibility for each other
questions.explanation: Each link joins a fact about Priestley to a choice in the play. Used this way, biography explains purpose.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses Priestley’s life to explain his purpose, rather than just adding a fact?
options: Priestley, who had fought in the trenches, makes Birling dismiss the chance of war so that the audience stops trusting him.
Priestley was born in 1894 and died in 1984.
Priestley was a socialist. Birling is a capitalist.
Priestley went to Cambridge after the war, which is interesting.
questions.explanation: The first sentence ties a fact to a choice in the play and its effect on the audience. The others leave the fact unconnected.

questions.prompt: Which of these claims about Priestley are safe to make in an essay?
options: He wrote the play at the end of the Second World War.
He gave the Postscripts talks in 1940.
He was wounded on a date every source agrees on.
An exact audience figure that every source agrees on.
questions.explanation: Sources disagree on the date of his wounding and on audience figures. Say he was wounded, and that millions listened, without a precise figure.
questions.misconception: Treating disputed dates and figures as settled facts.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph explaining how Priestley’s beliefs help to explain the Inspector’s final speech. Use context to explain purpose.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley was a socialist who helped to found the Common Wealth party in 1942 and who, in his Postscripts talks of 1940, spoke to millions about a fairer Britain after the war. The Inspector’s final speech carries those beliefs onto the stage: his insistence that “We are responsible for each other” (Inspector, Act 3) replaces Birling’s idea that a man need only look after himself. Because the speech turns from the family to everyone, it sounds like a broadcast to the nation, and Priestley’s audience in 1945, voting on what kind of country to build, is invited to take the warning personally.
checklist: Gives accurate context about Priestley’s socialism or Postscripts
Links the context to a specific moment: the final speech
Explains the purpose or effect on the 1945 audience
Uses a short, accurate reference to the speech
Avoids disputed claims such as why the talks ended
questions.explanation: Context should explain why Priestley wrote the speech as he did, not sit beside it as a separate fact.

units.title: Britain in 1912: the world of the play
units.summary: The play is set in 1912, in a society divided by class, with no welfare state and no vote for women. The Titanic and the coming war give the audience hindsight.

questions.prompt: In what year is An Inspector Calls set?
questions.explanation: The play is set in 1912 and first performed in 1945. Mixing up the setting and the date of writing is a common slip.
questions.misconception: Confusing the date of the setting with the date of writing.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about 1912 is true or false.

statements.s: No woman could vote in a general election.
There was a welfare state to support people out of work.
A factory worker could be sacked with no notice.
The First World War had already begun.

questions.explanation: War began in 1914, 2 years after the setting. Help for people with no work depended largely on charity.

questions.prompt: Women over 30 who met a property qualification gained the vote in ___. Women won the vote on the same terms as men in ___.
questions.explanation: Both dates come after the play’s setting, so Eva and Sheila have no vote at all in 1912.

questions.prompt: When did the Titanic sink?
questions.explanation: It left Southampton on 10 April 1912, struck an iceberg late on 14 April and sank early on 15 April. About 1,500 people died.

questions.prompt: Match each 1912 fact to a moment in the play.
pairs: Employers could sack workers at will
Milwards dismisses Eva after Sheila complains
Help for the poor came from charities
Women were judged by their reputation
Gerald’s affair is treated as forgivable
questions.explanation: Each fact explains why one character could harm Eva so easily. Context works best when it is tied to a moment like this.

questions.prompt: Why did Mrs Birling’s charity committee have so much power over Eva?
options: With no welfare state, a woman with no job or family had almost nowhere else to turn.
Charities were run by the police.
Eva was a member of the committee.
The law required Eva to obey the committee.
questions.explanation: In 1912 help for people with no work or money depended largely on charity, so a refusal could leave a pregnant woman with nothing.

questions.prompt: Birling hopes to rise in society. Which detail shows this?
options: He married his “social superior” (stage direction, Act 1) and welcomes Sheila’s engagement to Gerald, son of Sir George and Lady Croft.
He refuses to talk about business at dinner.
questions.explanation: Rich manufacturers like Birling wanted to be accepted by the old families. Both marriages help him climb.
questions.misconception: Treating all wealthy characters as the same class.

questions.prompt: By how much does Birling say the strikers’ demand would have added to his labour costs?
questions.explanation: He says agreeing would have added about 12% to his labour costs. Be precise with figures and never invent wages the play does not give.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses 1912 context most effectively?
options: Because a shop worker in 1912 could be sacked at once, Sheila’s passing bad temper is enough to end Eva’s job, which shows how much power the rich held over the poor.
In 1912 there was no welfare state. Women could not vote. Sheila gets Eva sacked.
Sheila gets Eva sacked. This was a long time ago.
In 1912 the Titanic sank and many people died, which is very sad.
questions.explanation: The first sentence uses the fact to explain a specific moment and what it shows. The others list facts that are never connected to the play.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley uses the year 1912 to shape his audience’s view of Birling. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley sets the play in 1912 so that his audience knows more than Birling does. When Birling calls the Titanic “unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable” (Birling, Act 1), the audience knows it sank that April, and when he dismisses the chance of war they know it came in 1914. The dramatic irony makes him look foolish, and because he is wrong about the future, the audience learns to distrust his views on workers and community too. The setting also lets Priestley show a world with no welfare state, where an employer like Birling could sack a worker without notice, so the audience sees how much damage such confidence could do.
checklist: Explains the audience’s hindsight about the Titanic and the war
Names dramatic irony and its effect on how Birling is judged
Links the irony to Birling’s wider views
Uses accurate 1912 context such as no welfare state
Keeps the focus on Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: The strongest answers show the 1912 setting doing a job: it turns Birling’s certainty into evidence against him.

units.title: Britain in 1945: the world of the audience
units.summary: Priestley wrote for an audience that had survived 2 world wars and had just voted for change. The 1912 setting lets that audience judge the Birlings with hindsight.

questions.prompt: Which party won the general election of July 1945?
questions.explanation: Labour won a landslide: 393 seats to the Conservatives’ 197. The country voted for reform as the war ended.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Priestley’s first audiences had lived through 2 world wars.
The National Health Service began on 5 July 1948.
William Beveridge’s report set out a plan for social security.
Priestley’s audience is best described as Victorian.

questions.explanation: The audience was a post-war one in 1945 and 1946. Pearson’s 2025 report noted students calling the audience Victorian or Jacobean.

questions.prompt: When was the play written?
options: At the end of the Second World War, usually dated 1944 to 1945
questions.explanation: Sources disagree about the exact months, so the safe wording is 1944 to 1945, at the end of the war.
questions.misconception: Giving a precise month of writing that sources dispute.

questions.prompt: How many seats did Labour win in the 1945 general election?
questions.explanation: Labour won 393 seats to the Conservatives’ 197. Use the figure only if it sharpens a point about the country voting for change.

questions.prompt: What did the Beveridge report of 1942 propose?
options: A plan for social security for everyone
A new party called Common Wealth
questions.explanation: The report set out a plan for social security. The welfare state that followed is responsibility shared by everyone, which is the Inspector’s idea.

questions.prompt: Match each area of life to how it had changed between 1912 and 1945.
pairs: From no vote to voting on equal terms since 1928
From charity deciding who got help to a planned welfare state
From rigid divisions to a war effort that brought classes closer
From employers like Birling in charge to a Labour landslide
questions.explanation: These contrasts explain why a 1945 audience could judge the Birlings’ world so clearly. Each one can sharpen a point about a moment in the play.

questions.prompt: Why might a 1945 audience hear the Inspector’s warning of “fire and blood and anguish” (Inspector, Act 3) so strongly?
options: They had lived through 2 world wars since 1912.
They had never heard of war.
The play was performed during the First World War.
The Inspector names the Second World War directly.
questions.explanation: The warning sounds like prophecy because the audience had survived the wars that followed 1912. The Inspector names neither war.

questions.prompt: Which phrase avoids the common slip examiners reported about dates?
options: The Jacobean audience of the play
The 1912 audience who watched it first
questions.explanation: Name both dates accurately. The play was first seen in 1945, though it is set in 1912.
questions.misconception: Calling the audience Victorian or Jacobean.

questions.prompt: Priestley invites his audience to side with Sheila and Eric. What does this suggest about his purpose in 1945?
options: He hoped the post-war generation would build a fairer country.
He wanted Britain to return to 1912.
He believed the young should obey their parents.
He thought politics did not matter.
questions.explanation: The older Birlings refuse to learn while the young begin to change. In 1945 the country had a real choice about what to build.

questions.prompt: Explain why Priestley set a play written in 1945 in the year 1912. Write 1 paragraph using context to explain his purpose.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Writing in 1945 about 1912, Priestley lets his audience see what Birling cannot. They knew the Titanic sank and that 2 world wars followed, so Birling’s confident lectures look dangerously wrong. The 1912 world also has no welfare state: Eva depends on employers and on Mrs Birling’s charity, and each of them fails her. An audience that had just voted Labour in a landslide, and was watching plans for social security take shape, is invited to see the Birlings’ world as the one Britain was leaving behind, and to make sure it did not come back.
checklist: Names both dates accurately
Explains the hindsight the audience has
Links the 1912 lack of welfare to a moment in the play
Uses 1945 context such as the election or the Beveridge plan
States Priestley’s purpose clearly
questions.explanation: The setting is a choice. Explaining what the gap between 1912 and 1945 does is what earns AO3 credit.

units.title: The play on stage: 1945, 1946 and 1992
units.summary: The play was first performed in the Soviet Union in 1945 and reached London in 1946. Stephen Daldry’s 1992 National Theatre production still shapes how many people see it.

questions.prompt: In which country was An Inspector Calls first performed?
questions.explanation: It was first performed in 1945 in Moscow and Leningrad. The exact month is disputed, so the year is enough.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The first London production opened on 1 October 1946.
Ralph Richardson played the Inspector in 1946.
Alec Guinness played Gerald in 1946.
Stephen Daldry directed a new production at the National Theatre in 1992.

questions.explanation: Alec Guinness played Eric in the 1946 London production. Daldry’s production opened at the National Theatre in 1992.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Priestley, did the play open abroad rather than in Britain?
options: He said no suitable theatre was available in Britain.
British actors refused to perform it.
questions.explanation: The guide hedges this: it is what Priestley said, not an established fact. Present it as his explanation.
questions.misconception: Stating Priestley’s own explanation as established fact.

questions.prompt: Daldry’s production turns the Birlings’ home into a doll’s house standing on what?
questions.explanation: The house stands on stilts in a bleak wasteland, cut off from the townspeople below.

questions.prompt: What does the raised house in Daldry’s production suggest about the Birlings?
options: They are cut off from the town and the people below them.
They are kind to their neighbours.
questions.explanation: Standing above the street, the house makes the family look isolated, and it collapses as their story falls apart.

questions.prompt: Match each production detail to what it adds.
pairs: Townspeople in 1940s clothes watch from outside
The audience sees 1912 and wartime Britain together
The family’s world falls apart visibly
Edna is played as an older woman
A link between 1912 and the future
questions.explanation: Each choice turns an idea in the script into something the audience sees. Link any staging point back to the text.

questions.prompt: What did Daldry’s production cut from Birling’s opening speech?
options: Part of it, including the Titanic line
questions.explanation: The production cut part of Birling’s opening speech, including the Titanic line. If you quote the Titanic line, you are quoting Priestley’s script.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The house falls down, so Priestley shows the family collapsing.’ What is wrong with this?
options: The collapsing house is Daldry’s staging, not something Priestley wrote, so the student should name the production.
The house never falls down in any production.
questions.explanation: Examiners want the play as Priestley wrote it. A production can support a point, but you should say which production and link it to the script.
questions.misconception: Treating a director’s choice as Priestley’s own writing.

questions.prompt: Daldry said he had heard that Priestley disliked seeing the play in a realistic box set. How does this help a student?
options: It shows a production can challenge how a play is staged, while the script stays the same.
It proves Priestley hated the play.
It means students must not mention stage directions.
It shows the play is set in 1992.
questions.explanation: Daldry wanted to return the play to a more radical tradition. That is a reading of the play in performance, which can support but not replace the text.

questions.prompt: Explain how a production choice can support a point about the play. Use Daldry’s 1992 production and link it to the script.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley’s stage directions describe a dining room that is “heavily comfortable” (stage direction, Act 1), a room built to show off wealth. In Stephen Daldry’s 1992 National Theatre production the house is raised on stilts above a wasteland, which makes the same point visually: the Birlings are cut off from the town whose workers pay for their comfort. When the house tilts and collapses as their story falls apart, the audience sees the family’s security being destroyed. The production supports what the script already suggests, that the Birlings’ protected world cannot keep the outside out.
checklist: Names the production and its date
Describes a specific staging choice accurately
Links the staging back to something in Priestley’s script
Explains the effect on the audience
Keeps the script, not the production, at the centre
questions.explanation: A production point earns credit when it is clearly labelled and tied back to the text.

units.title: Using context without bolting it on
units.summary: Context earns credit when it explains what Priestley is doing and why. Weave a short, relevant fact into your point about a moment instead of adding a history lesson.

questions.prompt: When does context earn the most credit?
options: When it explains Priestley’s purpose in a specific moment
When it fills a whole paragraph at the end
When it lists as many dates as possible
When it is about any period of history
questions.explanation: Examiners keep making the same point: context that helps explain what Priestley is doing and why is rewarded.

questions.prompt: What is ‘bolted-on’ context?
options: True facts added at the end of a paragraph, unconnected to the point
Context taken from the stage directions
questions.explanation: The facts may be accurate, but if they sit apart from the argument they earn very little.
questions.misconception: Thinking any accurate fact earns AO3 marks.

questions.prompt: Match each question focus to the most useful context.
pairs: No vote in 1912; few jobs for working-class women
Postscripts and the welfare state as shared responsibility
A post-war hope that the young would build a fairer Britain
questions.explanation: Choose the context the question points to. A fact about the vote helps a gender question far more than a class question.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about context and the boards is true or false.

statements.s: Edexcel gives 16 of its 40 marks to context.
Eduqas gives no marks for context on this question.
OCR rewards context in part (b).
AQA gives 6 of its 30 marks to context.

questions.explanation: OCR rewards context in part (a), the comparison, but not in part (b). The other statements match each board’s mark scheme.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2025 report noted answers about ‘the evils of the bourgeoisie’. What was the problem?
options: Big political words were never tied to evidence from the play.
Edexcel does not allow political ideas.
questions.explanation: Show the idea through a moment, such as Birling sacking the strike leaders, instead of using slogans.
questions.misconception: Using political labels without evidence from the play.

questions.prompt: Which sentence weaves context in rather than bolting it on?
options: Birling sacks the strike leaders without a second thought, and in a 1912 world with no welfare state that decision leaves Eva with nothing.
Birling sacks Eva. He is selfish. In 1912 there was no welfare state.
There was no welfare state in 1912. Women could not vote until 1918.
Birling is a capitalist. Capitalism is an economic system.
questions.explanation: The first sentence uses the fact to explain the effect of Birling’s decision on Eva. The others leave the fact standing alone.

questions.prompt: Birling calls keeping wages low “my duty to keep labour costs down” (Birling, Act 1). Which context best sharpens a comment on this line?
options: A 1945 audience had just voted for a welfare state, so they would see how much power this kind of ‘duty’ gave employers.
questions.explanation: The 1945 election links directly to Birling’s view of workers. The other facts are true but do not explain this line.

questions.prompt: An Edexcel student writes a full page on the history of the welfare state before mentioning the play. What would Pearson’s examiners say?
options: Context should run through the essay in short, specific points, not dominate it.
This is ideal because context is 16 marks.
Context is not rewarded on Edexcel.
The student should write 2 pages instead.
questions.explanation: Even a strong answer was told its context became ‘a little lengthy at times’ in Pearson’s 2019 report. Keep each point to a sentence or 2.

questions.prompt: Rewrite this paragraph so that the context explains Priestley’s purpose: ‘Mrs Birling refuses to help Eva. She is a snob. In 1912 there was no welfare state and charities helped the poor.’
questions.model: Model paragraph: Mrs Birling persuades her committee to refuse a pregnant girl who has used the Birling name, and Priestley makes sure the audience understands what that refusal meant. In 1912 there was no welfare state, so help for a woman with no work and no family depended on charity, and on the judgement of women like Mrs Birling. Priestley’s audience, watching the country plan social security for everyone, would see how cruel it was for help to be a favour handed out by people who judged the poor by class.
checklist: Starts from the moment in the play, not from the history
Ties the lack of a welfare state to Eva’s situation
Explains the effect on Priestley’s 1945 audience
Removes the label ‘snob’ and replaces it with analysis
Keeps context to 1 or 2 sentences
questions.explanation: Strong rewrites move the context into the middle of the point, where it explains why the moment matters.

questions.prompt: Which of these would be the weakest use of context in an answer on Sheila?
options: In 1912 there were suffragettes, and some of them broke windows.
Sheila’s complaint can end Eva’s job because shop workers in 1912 could be sacked at once.
Sheila’s change matters because Priestley’s 1945 audience hoped the young would build a fairer country.
With no vote, a woman like Eva had no say in the system that left her unprotected.
questions.explanation: A fact about suffragettes with no link to Sheila is the kind of list AQA’s 2020 report warned about. The other options tie context to the play.
questions.misconception: Listing facts about the period with no link to the play.

units.title: Act 1: the celebration dinner
units.summary: The play opens on a comfortable family party for Sheila’s engagement. Birling lectures the young men with confident predictions until the doorbell interrupts him.

questions.prompt: What event are the Birlings and Gerald celebrating when the play opens?
questions.explanation: They are finishing a dinner to celebrate Sheila’s engagement. Birling only hints that he may be given a knighthood.

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs Birling tell her husband off during the dinner?
options: He talks about business in his toast.
questions.explanation: Birling turns his toast towards Crofts and Birlings working together. Even at a celebration his mind is on profit.

questions.prompt: Put these Act 1 events in the order they happen.
items: Birling makes a toast that turns to business
Gerald gives Sheila her engagement ring
Birling tells the young people there will be no war
Birling confides to Gerald that he may get a knighthood
The doorbell rings during Birling’s speech
questions.explanation: The confident lectures build up until the doorbell cuts across them. Priestley lets Birling talk without interruption before the Inspector arrives.

questions.prompt: Who says “community and all that nonsense” (Act 1)?
questions.explanation: Birling dismisses community just before the doorbell rings. The Inspector has come to argue the very idea he mocks.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the opening is true or false.

statements.s: The lighting at the start is soft and pink.
Edna, the maid, is on stage in the opening moments.
Birling predicts that war is coming soon.
Eric is the one who announces the Inspector.

questions.explanation: Birling says there will be no war, and Edna announces the Inspector. The pink lighting suits the family’s comfortable view of itself.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley make the doorbell ring in the middle of Birling’s speech about looking after yourself?
options: To show that the Inspector has come to challenge exactly that belief
To give the actors a rest
To show that Edna is lazy
questions.explanation: The timing makes the Inspector’s arrival feel like an answer to Birling. From this point Birling is never fully in control again.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Birling’s predictions about the Titanic are just there to make the audience laugh.’ What does this miss?
options: The dramatic irony teaches the audience to distrust Birling before the Inspector arrives.
Birling is right about the Titanic.
Nothing: the lines have no other purpose.
questions.explanation: The comedy is serious. A man so wrong about the future is unlikely to be right about how to treat workers.
questions.misconception: Treating dramatic irony as comedy only.

questions.prompt: Which details in the opening hint at secrets to come?
options: Sheila teases Gerald about last summer, when he hardly came near her.
Eric is awkward and has been drinking.
Mrs Birling corrects her husband’s manners.
questions.explanation: Gerald’s absence last summer and Eric’s drinking both become part of the confessions. The other details show character but hide no secret.
questions.misconception: Missing the small tensions Priestley plants early.

questions.prompt: Which sentence treats Birling as Priestley’s construct rather than a real person?
options: Priestley gives Birling long, confident speeches so that the audience is ready to reject his views when the Inspector arrives.
Birling is a boring dad who talks too much at dinner.
Birling should have listened to his wife.
Birling is really proud of his daughter.
questions.explanation: The first sentence explains a choice Priestley made and its effect. The others judge Birling as if he were someone we know.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use the opening of Act 1 to prepare the audience for what follows? Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley opens with a family that is pleased with itself, so that the audience can watch that comfort break. Birling’s toast looks forward to the Crofts and Birlings working together “for lower costs and higher prices” (Birling, Act 1), which shows that profit comes first even at his daughter’s engagement. His confident claims about war and the Titanic are dramatic irony, because the 1945 audience knows both are wrong, and they learn to distrust him. Small tensions, such as Sheila’s teasing about last summer and Eric’s drinking, hint at secrets. When the doorbell interrupts Birling’s speech about looking after yourself, Priestley signals that this belief is about to be tested.
checklist: Explains that the comfortable opening is set up to be broken
Uses a short reference to Birling’s toast or speeches
Explains the dramatic irony and its effect
Notes the hints of secrets to come
Comments on the timing of the doorbell
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains what each part of the opening does for the rest of the play.

units.title: Act 1: the Inspector, Birling and Sheila
units.summary: The Inspector reports a young woman’s death and questions Birling, then Sheila. Birling refuses any responsibility; Sheila is ashamed at once.

questions.prompt: How does the Inspector say the young woman died?
options: She swallowed disinfectant and died in the Infirmary.
She was hit by a tram.
She died in a factory fire.
questions.explanation: He tells the family she died in the Infirmary 2 hours earlier, after swallowing disinfectant.

questions.prompt: What had Eva done at Birling’s works shortly before she lost her job there?
options: Helped to lead a strike for higher wages
questions.explanation: She was one of the leaders of a strike, and Birling sacked the leaders. Asking for a fair wage is the first link in the chain.

questions.prompt: Put these Act 1 events in order.
items: The Inspector arrives and the lighting becomes harsher
He shows a photograph to Birling alone
Birling insists he can accept no responsibility
The Inspector explains that Eva was out of work for 2 months
Sheila sees the photograph and runs out
Sheila admits having the shop assistant dismissed
questions.explanation: Birling’s questioning comes first and Sheila’s follows. The Inspector keeps control by showing the photograph to 1 person at a time.

questions.prompt: Who speaks of “a chain of events” (Act 1) that led to Eva’s death?
questions.explanation: The Inspector’s image explains both Eva’s death and the shape of his investigation, with each link leading to the next person.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The Inspector shows the photograph to Birling alone.
Eva was out of work for 2 months after leaving Birling’s works.
Eric agrees with his father that the strikers were wrong.
Sheila complained because she thought the shop assistant had smiled at her.

questions.explanation: Eric asks why the workers should not try for higher wages, which angers his father. Sheila’s complaint came from jealousy and bad temper.

questions.prompt: Why does the Inspector show the photograph to only 1 person at a time?
options: It keeps control of the questioning and lets each confession happen privately first.
He has lost the other copies.
The law forbids showing it to a group.
He wants the family to argue about who saw it.
questions.explanation: The method controls pace. It also gives Gerald the idea in Act 3 that each of them may have seen a different girl.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the photograph is accurate?
options: It is shown to 1 person at a time, so no one can be sure the others saw the same girl.
It is passed round the table for everyone to see at once.
Only Gerald is allowed to see it.
questions.explanation: A common mistake is to say everyone sees it together. The 1-at-a-time method matters to Gerald’s later theory.
questions.misconception: Saying the photograph is shown to everyone at once.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their first reaction in Act 1.
pairs: Promises never to do such a thing again
Asks why workers should not try for higher wages
Describes the death as a chain of links
questions.explanation: The reactions set up the split between the generations. Birling digs in while the younger characters start to question.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley place Birling’s confession and Sheila’s side by side in Act 1?
options: Their opposite responses set up the split between older and younger characters.
They are both about the Titanic.
Sheila and Birling did the same thing to Eva.
To show that Sheila is like her father.
questions.explanation: Birling refuses responsibility while Sheila feels it at once. The contrast decides how the ending sorts the characters.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley contrast Birling and Sheila in Act 1? Write 1 paragraph with at least 1 short quotation.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley sets Birling and Sheila side by side so that the audience can compare 2 responses to the same death. Birling’s first words on the matter, “I can’t accept any responsibility” (Birling, Act 1), show a man who measures everything by his business and refuses to see the girl as his concern. Sheila, by contrast, runs from the room when she sees the photograph and returns ready to admit that she used her position as a good customer to have the girl sacked. Her shame is immediate. Priestley uses the pair to show that change is possible for the young, while the older generation digs in.
checklist: Makes a clear comparative point
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains Sheila’s reaction with detail from the play
Links the contrast to the split between generations
Writes about Priestley’s purpose, not just the characters
questions.explanation: The contrast is a deliberate choice, and the best answers explain what Priestley gains from it.

units.title: End of Act 1 and Act 2: Gerald and Daisy Renton
units.summary: The new name Daisy Renton exposes Gerald’s affair. Act 1 ends on a cliffhanger, and in Act 2 Gerald tells his story and Sheila returns the ring.

questions.prompt: The Inspector says Eva changed her name, and Gerald is startled. What was her new name?
questions.explanation: Gerald knew her as Daisy Renton. His reaction gives him away before he admits anything.

questions.prompt: Where was Alderman Meggarty pestering Daisy when Gerald stepped in?
questions.explanation: Gerald met her at the Palace bar in March of the year before. Eric later meets her there too.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: The Inspector reveals that Eva took a new name
Gerald admits to Sheila, alone, that he knew her
The Inspector reappears in the doorway and the curtain falls
Mrs Birling enters, sure she can manage the Inspector
Gerald gives his account of the affair
Sheila gives back the ring and Gerald goes out for a walk
questions.explanation: The private admission comes at the end of Act 1 and the public account in Act 2. Splitting the confession across the act break builds suspense.

questions.prompt: Who calls Alderman Meggarty “a notorious womaniser” (Act 2)?
questions.explanation: Gerald condemns another man for preying on women while telling a story in which he keeps a mistress himself.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Gerald moved Daisy into a friend’s empty rooms and gave her money.
After the affair ended, Daisy went away to the seaside for 2 months.
Gerald met Daisy in March of the year before the play.
Sheila throws the ring at Gerald in anger.

questions.explanation: Sheila says she respects Gerald for telling the truth, but she gives the ring back calmly. It is her first independent decision.

questions.prompt: Why does Sheila say she respects Gerald, even though she returns the ring?
options: He has told the truth about the affair.
He promises to marry her the next day.
questions.explanation: His honesty earns some respect, yet she still breaks the engagement. Priestley shows her judging for herself.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of ending Act 1 with the Inspector reappearing and asking a 1-word question?
options: It is a cliffhanger: the audience wonders how much he knows about Gerald.
It resolves the mystery of Eva’s death.
It shows the Inspector has given up.
It tells the audience the play is over.
questions.explanation: Sheila has just warned Gerald that the Inspector already knows. The curtain falls on that tension.

questions.prompt: Which character kept Eva, as Daisy Renton, as his mistress?
questions.explanation: Gerald kept Daisy as his mistress; Eric made Eva pregnant and gave her stolen money. Examiners in 2025 reported answers that mixed up the 2 young men.
questions.misconception: Confusing Eric’s story with Gerald’s.

questions.prompt: Sheila calls Gerald her “fairy prince” (Act 2). What does this sarcasm suggest?
options: She sees through Gerald’s version of himself as Daisy’s rescuer.
She thinks Gerald is a real hero.
She is joking because she is drunk.
She wants Gerald to rescue her.
questions.explanation: The fairy-tale image mocks the idea that Gerald was simply being kind. Sheila refuses the role of the grateful woman.

questions.prompt: Is Gerald’s confession presented sympathetically? Write 1 paragraph that weighs both sides.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley makes Gerald the most sympathetic of the confessors, but not an innocent one. He rescued Daisy from Alderman Meggarty, found her rooms and gave her money, and he is the only one who did her some good. Yet he also made her his mistress and ended the affair when it suited him, and he tells the story in a way that flatters his own kindness. Sheila’s sarcasm punctures that version, and his decision to go out for a walk takes him away before the Inspector’s final speech. Priestley invites sympathy only to show that a kind rich man could still use a poor woman.
checklist: Gives evidence for sympathy: the rescue, the rooms, the money
Gives evidence against: the affair, ending it, hiding it
Notes how Gerald tells the story
Reaches a clear judgement
Writes about Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: A balanced answer still needs a clear view. Here the view is that sympathy is part of Priestley’s point.

units.title: Act 2: Mrs Birling and the charity
units.summary: Mrs Birling admits she persuaded her charity to refuse a pregnant girl, and demands that the father be punished. The act ends as Eric walks in.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the charity Mrs Birling helps to run?
questions.explanation: She is a leading member of the Brumley Women’s Charity Organisation, which gives her power over who receives help.

questions.prompt: Why was Mrs Birling offended by the girl who came to her committee?
options: The girl called herself Mrs Birling.
The girl was rude to Sheila.
The girl asked for a job.
The girl had stolen from the charity.
questions.explanation: Using the Birling name offended her, and after that nothing the girl said was believed.

questions.prompt: Put these Act 2 events in order.
items: The Inspector tells Birling that public figures have duties as well as advantages
Mrs Birling insists she did nothing she is ashamed of
The Inspector tells her she slammed the door in the girl’s face
She scorns the idea that the girl refused money
She demands that the father be found and made an example of
Eric comes in, pale and distressed
questions.explanation: Her denial hardens into demands, and those demands fall on her own son. The Inspector’s replies grow blunter as she grows more certain.

questions.prompt: Who says “Go and look for the father” (Act 2)?
questions.explanation: Mrs Birling gives the order to the Inspector. The audience realises before she does that the father is Eric.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Mrs Birling persuaded the whole committee to refuse the girl.
The girl came to the committee 2 weeks before the play.
Mrs Birling quickly accepts that she was wrong.
Gerald is in the room while Mrs Birling is questioned.

questions.explanation: Gerald has gone for a walk, and Mrs Birling never admits fault. She used her influence over the whole committee.

questions.prompt: What is the dramatic irony at the end of Act 2?
options: Mrs Birling demands punishment for the father without realising he is her son.
Birling predicts there will be no war.
The Inspector reveals he is a ghost.
Sheila does not know Gerald’s secret.
questions.explanation: The audience is ahead of her. Eric’s entrance completes the irony as the curtain falls.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the charity refusal is accurate?
options: Mrs Birling persuades the others, which shows how much influence one respected woman of her class had.
Mrs Birling refuses the girl alone, without the committee.
The girl never reaches the committee.
questions.explanation: Writing that she works alone misses the point: her status lets her sway the whole committee.
questions.misconception: Writing that Mrs Birling works alone.

questions.prompt: When Mrs Birling talks of what is proper for a girl in her position, the Inspector answers with a brutal image of the girl’s body. Why does Priestley write it this way?
options: To force the comfortable Mrs Birling to face the physical reality of the death
To show that the Inspector is a doctor
To prove the girl is still alive
questions.explanation: Plain physical language cuts through her polite talk of position. The Inspector will not let respectable words hide what happened.

questions.prompt: Match each moment in Act 2 to the method Priestley uses.
pairs: Mrs Birling demands that the father be punished
Eric enters as the curtain falls
The Inspector checks his watch as she condemns the father
A sign of his control and foreknowledge
The committee refuses the girl on Mrs Birling’s word
Charity shown as a kind of power
questions.explanation: Each moment is a choice by Priestley. Naming the method and its effect is how you turn plot into analysis.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use Mrs Birling’s questioning to build tension at the end of Act 2? Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley builds tension by letting the audience understand before Mrs Birling does. She dismisses the girl with “Girls of that class” (Mrs Birling, Act 2) and insists the real culprit is the young father, demanding that he be made an example of. The more certain she sounds, the more the audience dreads the moment she realises the father is Eric. Sheila’s pleading to stop adds pressure, and the Inspector’s calm control suggests he knows what is coming. When the front door is heard and Eric walks in, pale and distressed, the dramatic irony is complete and the act ends on a cliffhanger.
checklist: Explains the dramatic irony clearly
Uses a short, accurate reference to Mrs Birling’s words
Notes Sheila’s or the Inspector’s part in the tension
Comments on the timing of Eric’s entrance
Explains the effect on the audience
questions.explanation: Tension here comes from what the audience knows. The best answers explain how Priestley controls that gap.

units.title: Act 3: Eric’s story and the Inspector’s last words
units.summary: Eric confesses to getting Eva pregnant and stealing money for her. The Inspector sums up each person’s part and leaves after a warning to everyone.

questions.prompt: Whose confession comes last in the play?
questions.explanation: The order is Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Mrs Birling, Eric. Holding Eric back until last brings the family’s collapse and the final speech together.

questions.prompt: Why did Eva refuse to marry Eric?
options: She knew he did not love her.
She was already married to Gerald.
questions.explanation: She refused to marry him, knowing he did not love her, and she stopped taking his money when she learned it was stolen.

questions.prompt: Put these Act 3 events in order.
items: Eric confesses how he met Eva at the Palace bar
Birling is furious about the stolen money
Eric learns that his mother turned Eva away
The Inspector sums up what each of them did
The Inspector makes his final speech and leaves
questions.explanation: Eric’s confession sets father and son, then mother and son, against each other. Only then does the Inspector deliver his summing-up.

questions.prompt: Who admits that “a chap easily turns nasty” (Act 3)?
questions.explanation: Eric admits this about the night he was drunk and pressured Eva into letting him into her lodgings. His informal language makes the confession raw.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Eric is the only character who clearly broke the law.
Gerald hears the Inspector’s final speech.
Eva stopped taking Eric’s money when she found out it was stolen.
The Inspector arrests Eric before he leaves.

questions.explanation: Gerald is out of the house for the final speech, and no one is arrested. Eric’s theft is the one clear crime.

questions.prompt: In his final speech the Inspector moves from speaking about ‘you’ to speaking about ‘we’. What is the effect?
options: The message now includes everyone, including the audience.
He is admitting his own guilt for Eva’s death.
He is talking only to Sheila.
He has forgotten who is in the room.
questions.explanation: Moving from accusing individuals to speaking of everyone turns the speech outwards to the audience.

questions.prompt: A 1945 audience heard the speech end with a warning of suffering. Why would this strike so hard?
options: They had lived through 2 world wars since 1912.
They knew the Inspector was real.
questions.explanation: The warning sounds like prophecy to people who had survived the wars that followed. Priestley names no war directly.
questions.misconception: Assuming the speech refers to a named war.

questions.prompt: Which is the better way to use the final speech in an exam?
options: Quote 1 short phrase and analyse its method, such as the move from 1 girl to millions.
Write out as much of the speech as you can remember.
Avoid it because it is too famous.
questions.explanation: A long memorised chunk earns less than 1 phrase explained well. Examiners reward analysis, not length of quotation.
questions.misconception: Believing long memorised quotations earn more marks.

questions.prompt: Which sentence treats Eric as a construct rather than a real person?
options: Priestley gives Eric the most disturbing confession so that the audience cannot simply admire his change.
Eric is a horrible person and should go to prison.
Eric is my least favourite character.
questions.explanation: The first sentence explains a choice Priestley made and its effect on the audience. The others react to Eric as if he were real.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley make the Inspector’s final speech persuasive? Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley makes the final speech persuasive by stripping it down to plain statements that sound impossible to argue with. The line “We are responsible for each other” (Inspector, Act 3) is short and declarative, and the pronoun ‘we’ includes the audience as well as the Birlings. The speech then widens from 1 girl to millions of ordinary working people, so Eva becomes a symbol of everyone whose life depends on the choices of the powerful. It ends with a warning of suffering, which a 1945 audience would connect with 2 world wars. The Inspector then leaves, so the warning hangs in the air.
checklist: Analyses the sentence forms or the pronoun ‘we’
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains how Eva becomes a symbol
Links the warning to the 1945 audience
Comments on the effect of the Inspector leaving straight after
questions.explanation: Persuasion comes from method. Strong answers name the method and explain how it works on the audience.

units.title: Act 3: was it a hoax?
units.summary: After the Inspector leaves, Gerald’s news suggests a hoax and the older characters relax. A final telephone call announces a death and an inspector on his way.

questions.prompt: Who brings back news from a police officer that there is no Inspector Goole on the force?
questions.explanation: Gerald returns from his walk with the news, and the Chief Constable confirms it when Birling telephones.

questions.prompt: What does the call to the Infirmary seem to show?
options: No girl has been brought in after drinking disinfectant.
Eva is still alive and well.
The Inspector works at the Infirmary.
questions.explanation: The call appears to confirm the hoax. The older Birlings and Gerald relax and joke.

questions.prompt: Put these Act 3 events in order.
items: The Inspector leaves after his final speech
Gerald returns with news from a police officer
The Chief Constable confirms there is no Inspector Goole
Gerald suggests they may each have seen a different girl
A call to the Infirmary finds no dead girl
questions.explanation: News, then confirmation, then a theory, then relief. Priestley lets the relief build before the final call destroys it.

questions.prompt: Who says “Everything’s all right now, Sheila” (Act 3)?
questions.explanation: Gerald says it as he offers Sheila the ring again. The telephone soon proves him wrong.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Sheila takes the ring back as soon as Gerald offers it.
The final call says that a police inspector is on his way.
Inspector Goole walks back on stage at the end.
Birling mocks the younger generation just before the call.

questions.explanation: Sheila will not take the ring yet, and the play stops before any inspector arrives. Birling is mocking his children when the telephone rings.

questions.prompt: Gerald suggests the family may each have been shown a different girl. What does this suggest about the older characters?
options: They badly want a way out of responsibility.
They want the Inspector to return.
questions.explanation: The theory gives them an escape. Priestley shows how hard the older characters work to avoid facing what they did.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the ending is accurate?
options: The play stops before the new police inspector arrives.
Inspector Goole returns and arrests Birling.
Gerald reveals he is the Inspector.
questions.explanation: The call announces that a police inspector is on his way. Saying Goole returns is a common mistake.
questions.misconception: Saying that Inspector Goole returns at the end.

questions.prompt: Which characters still accept responsibility after the hoax seems proved?
questions.explanation: Only Sheila and Eric refuse to pretend once they think they are safe. The hoax lets Priestley test every character.

questions.prompt: Why might Priestley never explain who the Inspector was?
options: The mystery keeps attention on what the family did rather than on his identity.
He forgot to finish the play.
questions.explanation: Whether or not he was a real inspector, the family’s actions were real. That is the question Priestley wants the audience to face.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use the hoax to test the characters? Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses the hoax to show who has really learned. Once Gerald’s news and the Infirmary call seem to prove the evening was a trick, the older Birlings and Gerald relax and joke, and Gerald offers Sheila the ring again. Their relief shows they cared about being caught, not about the girl. Sheila and Eric refuse to go back; Sheila warns her parents “You’re beginning to pretend” (Sheila, Act 3). By letting the characters believe they are safe, Priestley reveals what each of them values, and the final telephone call punishes those who chose to forget.
checklist: Explains how the hoax seems to be proved
Contrasts the older characters and Gerald with Sheila and Eric
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains what the relief reveals
Links to the final telephone call
questions.explanation: A test needs a choice. The best answers show how the hoax gives each character the chance to choose.

units.title: Eva Smith’s life as a chain of events
units.summary: Eva’s story covers about 2 years, from Birling’s factory to the Infirmary, but the family hear it in 1 evening. Each confession starts where the last one ended.

questions.prompt: Where does Eva’s story begin?
options: At Birling’s factory, where she helps lead a strike
questions.explanation: About 2 years before the play she worked at Birling’s factory. Her sacking after the strike is the first link.

questions.prompt: Name the department store where Eva worked after leaving the factory.
questions.explanation: She was dismissed from Milwards after Sheila complained about her.

questions.prompt: Put the events of Eva’s life in the order they happened.
items: She is sacked after the strike at Birling’s factory
She is dismissed from Milwards after Sheila complains
Calling herself Daisy Renton, she becomes Gerald’s mistress
She goes to the seaside for 2 months
She becomes pregnant by Eric
The charity committee refuses her help
She dies in the Infirmary
questions.explanation: This is the order of her life, which is also the order of the confessions except that Mrs Birling’s comes before Eric’s.

questions.prompt: Match each character to the power they had over Eva.
pairs: An employer’s power over wages and jobs
A wealthy customer’s power over a shop worker
A rich man’s power over a woman with no money
The power to decide who deserves charity
questions.explanation: Each kind of power is different, but each comes from wealth or class. Priestley shows a whole system working against her.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the order of Eva’s life is true or false.

statements.s: Eva met Gerald before she met Eric.
Eva worked at Milwards before she worked at Birling’s factory.
Eva went to the charity about 2 weeks before she died.
Eva went to the seaside after the affair with Gerald ended.

questions.explanation: The factory came first and Milwards second. Gerald’s affair ended before her time at the seaside, and Eric met her afterwards.

questions.prompt: Eva’s story covers about 2 years, yet the family hear it in 1 evening. What is the effect?
options: The pressure builds without a break as each part is revealed.
The audience loses track of time.
It shows the Inspector is lazy.
It makes the play feel slow.
questions.explanation: Compressing 2 years into 1 evening means revelation follows revelation. The family have no time to recover.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2024 report found weaker answers on Eva left out 1 character altogether. Which plan avoids that mistake?
options: Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Mrs Birling and Eric, each linked to the next
Mrs Birling and Eric only, as the most serious
Sheila only, because she is sorriest
questions.explanation: The report noted that weaker answers often left Gerald out. Follow all of Eva’s encounters.
questions.misconception: Leaving Gerald out of an answer on Eva.

questions.prompt: Why does the Inspector take the family through Eva’s story in the order it happened?
options: Each confession starts where the last ended, so the links in the chain become clear.
It is the order the family arrived home.
He wants to save the shortest story for last.
It follows the alphabetical order of their names.
questions.explanation: Moving through her life in order makes the chain visible. No single act killed her, but each one led to the next.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids treating Eva as a real person whose feelings we know?
options: Gerald claims Daisy was happy for a while, but Priestley gives this account to someone with reasons to tell it kindly.
Eva was really happy with Gerald.
questions.explanation: Eva never appears, so everything we hear comes from people who harmed her. Present her feelings as their claims.
questions.misconception: Treating Eva’s feelings as known facts.

questions.prompt: Explain how the chain-of-events structure supports Priestley’s message about responsibility.
questions.model: Model paragraph: The Inspector describes Eva’s death as “a chain of events” (Inspector, Act 1), and Priestley builds the play the same way. Each confession begins where the last one ended: Birling sacks her, Sheila has her dismissed from Milwards, Gerald takes her up and lets her go, Mrs Birling refuses her charity and Eric’s story fills in why she needed it. No single act killed her, so each character can claim innocence, yet together they destroyed her. The structure itself argues Priestley’s point: in a society, responsibility is shared, and people who see only their own link are blind to the whole chain.
checklist: Uses the chain image accurately
Shows how the confessions link in order
Explains why no single character is solely to blame
Connects the structure to Priestley’s message about shared responsibility
Keeps the focus on Priestley’s choices
questions.explanation: The structure is part of the argument. Strong answers show form and meaning working together.

units.title: The Inspector: who is he?
units.summary: Inspector Goole controls the questioning, is impossible to impress and leaves before anyone can prove who he is. Priestley leaves his identity open on purpose.

questions.prompt: Which word does the Inspector’s surname sound like?
questions.explanation: Goole sounds like ghoul. Pearson’s 2019 report noted that most students picked up on the name.

questions.prompt: Which member of the family does the Inspector question first?
questions.explanation: He starts with Birling, who sacked Eva first, and works through the family in the order of her life.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the Inspector do to keep control?
options: Shows the photograph to 1 person at a time
Cuts across Birling when he tries to take charge
Arrests each person after they confess
Checks his watch as Mrs Birling condemns the father
questions.explanation: He decides the order, refuses to be hurried and seems to know what is coming. He never arrests anyone.

questions.prompt: Match each reading of the Inspector to the evidence for it.
pairs: Possible, but the play gives this reading no support
Suggested by his name and the call that seems to predict the future
He makes the family face what they already know
He speaks for the playwright’s own beliefs
questions.explanation: Priestley leaves the question open. The strongest answers argue for a reading and show why the mystery helps his message.

questions.prompt: Who tells Mrs Birling “You slammed the door in her face” (Act 2)?
questions.explanation: The Inspector turns a committee decision into a plain physical image. He will not let polite language hide what happened.

questions.prompt: Why does the Inspector never arrest anyone?
options: Most of what the family did was not a crime; he judges them by a moral standard.
He plans to come back and arrest them later.
questions.explanation: Pearson’s 2019 report described answers that saw him as a moral rather than a legal figure. That is a strong way to write about him.

questions.prompt: Which approach to the question ‘Who is the Inspector?’ is strongest?
options: Argue for a reading and explain why the mystery helps Priestley’s message.
State that he is definitely a ghost and move on.
Say the question cannot be answered, so leave him out.
Prove he is a real policeman using the Chief Constable’s call.
questions.explanation: Any reading can be argued, but the best answers show why Priestley left him unexplained: the focus stays on what the family did.
questions.misconception: Treating the Inspector’s identity as a puzzle with 1 correct answer.

questions.prompt: The questioning gives the play the shape of a detective story. How does this detective differ from most?
options: He wants every suspect to admit a share of the guilt, not find 1 culprit.
He solves the case by finding fingerprints.
He accuses Edna of the crime.
questions.explanation: A death and a confession from each suspect in turn is the classic pattern, but here every suspect played a part.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the Inspector is true or false.

statements.s: He first appears just as Birling is praising self-interest.
He leaves before anyone can prove who he is.
He talks at length about his own family.
He lets Birling take charge of the questioning.

questions.explanation: He has no private life in the play and refuses to let Birling take over. His timing and control are part of Priestley’s design.

questions.prompt: Who is the Inspector? Write a paragraph that argues for 1 reading and explains why Priestley leaves the question open.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley presents the Inspector as a conscience more than a policeman. He seems to know what each person did before they admit it, he shows the photograph to 1 person at a time so that each must face their own guilt, and he never arrests anyone because most of what the Birlings did was not a crime. His name, sounding like ghoul, and the final telephone call hint at something beyond the ordinary. By never explaining him, Priestley keeps attention on the family’s actions: whatever the Inspector was, the harm they did was real.
checklist: Argues for 1 clear reading
Supports it with details of how he behaves
Mentions his name or the ending as evidence
Explains why Priestley leaves the mystery unsolved
Treats the Inspector as Priestley’s creation
questions.explanation: The best answers turn an unanswerable question into a point about Priestley’s purpose.

units.title: The Inspector: Priestley’s device
units.summary: The Inspector has no private life: he exists to drive the plot and voice Priestley’s beliefs. Write ‘Priestley uses the Inspector to...’ to show you see the device.

questions.prompt: What is the Inspector’s main job in the play?
options: To drive the plot and say what Priestley wants the audience to hear
To fall in love with Sheila
questions.explanation: He has no family and no private life. Every character is a construct, but he is the clearest case.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The Inspector has no family or private life in the play.
Birling’s Act 1 speeches set out the opposite view to the Inspector’s.
By Act 3 the Inspector speaks only to Eric.
His final speech speaks to everyone, including the audience.

questions.explanation: By Act 3 he no longer answers individuals. The play becomes a debate between Birling’s view and his, which the Inspector wins.

questions.prompt: Birling fears that workers will soon be “asking for the earth” (Birling, Act 1). How does the Inspector answer him?
options: He turns the phrase round: asking is better than taking by force.
He agrees that workers ask for too much.
He says the strikers should be arrested.
questions.explanation: The Inspector reuses Birling’s phrase as a warning about what happens when people are denied too long.

questions.prompt: Match what the Inspector does to why Priestley needs it.
pairs: Sets up an argument between 2 views of society
Controls pace and gives each confession its own moment
Refuses to be impressed by rank
Shows that status is no excuse
Leaves before the hoax is discovered
Makes the family’s reactions the real test
questions.explanation: Each action has a dramatic purpose. Writing about the purpose is how you treat him as a device.

questions.prompt: The Inspector sums up: “each of you helped to kill her” (Inspector, Act 3). What do the words ‘each’ and ‘helped’ do together?
options: ‘Each’ insists on individual guilt and ‘helped’ on shared guilt.
They show he blames only Eric.
They show the death was an accident.
They make the line sound uncertain.
questions.explanation: The line holds both ideas at once, so no one is let off and no one can blame the others.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The Inspector thinks the Birlings are selfish.’ How could this be improved?
options: Write ‘Priestley uses the Inspector to expose the Birlings’ selfishness’.
Write ‘The Inspector really hates the Birlings’.
Remove the Inspector from the sentence.
Add more adjectives about the Inspector.
questions.explanation: Naming Priestley shows the examiner you understand the Inspector is a device with a purpose.
questions.misconception: Writing about characters as if they were real people.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley make the Inspector arrive just as Birling is praising self-interest?
options: It sets up the play as an argument between 2 views of society.
It is a coincidence with no meaning.
It gives Birling time to finish dinner.
It shows the Inspector was listening at the door.
questions.explanation: The entrance answers Birling’s view at the moment he states it. The rest of the play tests which view is right.

questions.prompt: The Inspector warns that people will be taught in “fire and blood and anguish” (Inspector, Act 3). What is the effect of the repeated ‘and’?
options: The warning builds in intensity, item by item.
It makes the warning sound casual.
It shows the Inspector is unsure.
It lists things the Birlings own.
questions.explanation: The repetition piles up the suffering. For a 1945 audience the warning pointed to the 2 world wars.

questions.prompt: Why does the Inspector leave before the hoax is discovered?
options: So that the family’s reactions, not his identity, become the real test
questions.explanation: Once he has gone, each character must decide alone whether the lesson still matters. That choice is Priestley’s test.

questions.prompt: Explore how Priestley uses the Inspector as a dramatic device. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses the Inspector as a moral judge rather than a policeman. He has no private life; he exists to question each character in turn and to answer Birling’s selfish speeches with Priestley’s own belief in shared responsibility. His control of the questioning, 1 person at a time, drives the plot and keeps suspense high, and his refusal to be impressed by rank shows that status is no excuse. By Act 3 he no longer answers individuals but speaks to everyone, so his final speech reaches past the Birlings to Priestley’s 1945 audience, who were deciding what kind of country to build.
checklist: Treats the Inspector as a device throughout
Explains how he drives the plot
Links his views to Priestley’s beliefs
Notes how the final speech addresses the audience
Uses relevant context about 1945
questions.explanation: Writing ‘Priestley uses the Inspector to...’ keeps the playwright in view, which is what examiners reward.

units.title: Arthur Birling
units.summary: Birling is a wealthy manufacturer, a former Lord Mayor and a magistrate who refuses to change. Priestley makes him pompous and wrong so the audience rejects his views.

questions.prompt: Which public role does Birling still hold when the play opens?
questions.explanation: He is a former Lord Mayor and still a magistrate. A man this wrong about the world sits in judgement on others.

questions.prompt: Why is Birling pleased about Sheila’s engagement?
options: It links his family and firm to the higher-ranking Crofts.
He likes Gerald’s sense of humour.
Gerald has promised to work in his factory.
It means Sheila will move away.
questions.explanation: Crofts Limited is older and bigger than his firm. The marriage is a business merger and a step up the social ladder.

questions.prompt: Match each trait to the evidence for it.
pairs: Reminds the Inspector that he used to be an alderman
Turns his engagement toast to costs and prices
Mocks his children as a generation who know it all
questions.explanation: Each trait is shown through what Birling says. Priestley gives the audience a clear target.

questions.prompt: Who mocks the idea that people are connected “like bees in a hive” (Act 1)?
questions.explanation: Birling mocks the idea in Act 1. The Inspector’s case will prove it true.

questions.prompt: Why is Birling’s bee image ironic?
options: He mocks the idea of people being connected, which the play then proves.
questions.explanation: Priestley gives Birling an image he means as a joke, and the chain of events turns it into the truth.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about Birling in Act 3 is true or false.

statements.s: He worries about scandal and his knighthood.
He is delighted when the Inspector seems to be a fraud.
He accepts responsibility and apologises to his children.
He is laughing at his children when the telephone rings.

questions.explanation: Birling learns nothing. The final call catches him at the moment he is mocking the young, which is how Priestley punishes him.

questions.prompt: A student argues that Birling is only a comic figure. What is the stronger view?
options: He is funny at first, but a man this wrong runs a factory and sits as a magistrate, so his views are dangerous.
He is purely comic and has no other role.
He is the hero of the play.
He is a tragic figure who learns too late.
questions.explanation: Priestley makes the comedy serious: Birling has power over people like Eva.
questions.misconception: Seeing Birling only as comic relief.

questions.prompt: Birling calls keeping wages low his duty. What does the word duty do?
options: It dresses up self-interest as a moral principle.
It shows he cares about his workers.
It shows he is a police officer.
It shows he wants to raise wages.
questions.explanation: By calling it duty he never has to feel guilty. The Inspector later uses the language of duty against the family.

questions.prompt: AQA’s examiners praised answers that discussed Birling as a device. Which sentence does this?
options: Priestley uses Birling to give the audience a clear target: the attitudes he wanted Britain to leave behind in 1945.
Birling is a horrible man who only cares about money.
I would not like Birling as a dad.
Birling deserves to lose his business.
questions.explanation: The first sentence asks what Birling is for. The others react to him as if he were a real person.
questions.misconception: Writing about characters as if they were real people.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley turns Birling into a warning to his audience about society. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley makes Birling pompous and wrong so that the audience rejects the selfish capitalism he stands for. He sees himself as a “hard-headed” (Birling, Act 1) man of business, yet his confident predictions about war and the Titanic are proved false by history, and the audience learns to doubt him. He sacked Eva for asking for a fair wage and calls keeping costs down his duty. Above all, he never changes: in Act 3 he worries about scandal, not the girl. By catching him out with the final telephone call, Priestley warns his 1945 audience what happens if men like Birling stay in charge.
checklist: Makes a clear argument about Priestley’s purpose
Uses a short, accurate reference
Comments on dramatic irony
Shows that Birling does not change
Links to the 1945 audience
questions.explanation: Strong answers explain what Birling is for, not just what he is like.

units.title: Sybil Birling
units.summary: Mrs Birling is cold and sure of her own superiority. She uses her charity to refuse Eva and never admits she was wrong, while her own words condemn her son.

questions.prompt: What do the stage directions say about Mrs Birling’s class compared with her husband’s?
options: She is from a poorer family.
They are from exactly the same background.
questions.explanation: She comes from a higher class than Birling. This is a key to both characters and to his social climbing.

questions.prompt: What was Mrs Birling’s part in Eva’s story?
options: She persuaded her charity to refuse Eva help when she was pregnant.
She sacked Eva from the factory.
She had Eva dismissed from Milwards.
questions.explanation: Her refusal came about 2 weeks before Eva’s death, when Eva had nowhere else to go.

questions.prompt: Who calls Sheila a “hysterical child” (Act 2)?
questions.explanation: Mrs Birling says it when Sheila begs her to stop. Some revision sources give the line to Birling, but it is Mrs Birling’s.
questions.misconception: Giving the line to Birling.

questions.prompt: Match each trait to the evidence for it.
pairs: Judges Eva by her class before knowing anything about her
Insists she did nothing to be ashamed of
Orders the Inspector to find the father
Calls her daughter childish when she pleads
questions.explanation: Each trait shows a woman who measures others by her own rules and finds nothing wrong with herself.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use the charity to make a point about class?
options: It shows charity working as power, handed out by people who judge the poor by their own standards.
It shows the rich were always generous.
It shows charities were run by the government.
It shows Mrs Birling secretly wanted to help.
questions.explanation: The committee should help women in need, but Mrs Birling decides who is deserving.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The girl offended Mrs Birling by calling herself Mrs Birling.
Mrs Birling never admits that she was wrong.
She realises from the start that the father is Eric.
Sheila stops calling her Mummy and calls her Mother later.
