questions.explanation: The audience works out that Eric is the father before she does. That gap is the dramatic irony of the end of Act 2.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2023 examiners rewarded answers that looked past simple snobbery. What deeper reading did they credit?
options: Her refusal may also be self-protection: she cannot afford a link with a pregnant girl using her name.
She is secretly kind and regrets nothing.
She did not understand what the girl wanted.
questions.explanation: This does not excuse her, but it helps explain her choices. It is a more developed reading than ‘she is a snob’.
questions.misconception: Seeing only 1 simple motive in Mrs Birling.

questions.prompt: Why is Mrs Birling’s demand that the father be punished so damaging to her?
options: The father turns out to be her son, so her own words condemn her family.
It is against the law to demand punishment.
questions.explanation: Priestley uses dramatic irony so that her confident moral language collapses back on her.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley set Mrs Birling against Sheila?
options: To show 2 generations of women: the mother never moves while the daughter changes
Because they are rivals for Gerald
To show they agree about everything
Because Sheila works for the charity
questions.explanation: The pair show the difference between the generations, which is central to Priestley’s hope in the young.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley uses Mrs Birling to show the danger of refusing responsibility. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley presents Mrs Birling as a woman whose class prejudice blinds her to her own guilt. She insists “I did nothing I’m ashamed of” (Mrs Birling, Act 2), measuring her conduct by her own rules and finding nothing wrong. Instead she places all the blame on the young father, demanding that he be made an example of. Priestley uses dramatic irony so that the audience realises before she does that the father is Eric, and her confident respectability collapses. For an audience in 1945, debating whether help should be a right, her power to refuse a pregnant girl would look especially cruel.
checklist: Makes a clear argument about refusing responsibility
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains the dramatic irony
Links to class or charity as power
Uses context to explain the effect on the audience
questions.explanation: The strongest answers show her refusal as Priestley’s target, not just a personality flaw.

units.title: Sheila Birling
units.summary: Sheila begins as a lively, rather spoilt daughter and becomes the character who changes most. She is the first to accept responsibility.

questions.prompt: What was Sheila’s part in Eva’s story?
options: She had Eva dismissed from Milwards.
She sacked Eva after the strike.
She kept Eva as a companion.
questions.explanation: In a bad temper she complained, and because she was a good customer the shop sacked the girl.

questions.prompt: What is Sheila’s turning point?
questions.explanation: From the moment she sees the photograph she begins to understand how the Inspector works.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of Sheila’s development in order.
items: Playful and pleased with her ring
Ashamed, she accepts her part at once
Warns her mother and returns the ring
Refuses to pretend once the hoax is suspected
questions.explanation: Her questions become sharper and less polite as the play goes on. The order tracks Acts 1 to 3.

questions.prompt: Who says “It’s too late” (Act 1) when Sheila says she would help the girl now if she could?
questions.explanation: The line is the Inspector’s flat reply to Sheila. Some revision sources give it to Sheila, but it is the Inspector who says it.
questions.misconception: Giving the Inspector’s reply to Sheila.

questions.prompt: What made Sheila complain about the assistant at Milwards?
options: She tried on a dress that did not suit her and thought the assistant smiled.
The assistant was rude to Mrs Birling.
The assistant refused to serve her.
questions.explanation: It is the smallest act in the chain, done in a moment of jealousy. She is the quickest to feel its weight.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Sheila is the first character to accept responsibility.
Sheila warns Gerald that the Inspector already knows.
Sheila defends her father’s treatment of the strikers.
Sheila urges her mother to stop condemning the father.

questions.explanation: Sheila rejects her father’s way of seeing workers from the start. She learns faster than anyone in the family.

questions.prompt: Sheila’s first response to Eva’s story is “These girls aren’t cheap labour” (Sheila, Act 1). What does it reject?
options: Her father’s way of seeing workers only as costs
Gerald’s story about the Palace bar
questions.explanation: The line insists that workers are people. Sheila takes the side the Inspector will argue for.

questions.prompt: Sheila’s action is the smallest in the chain. Why might Priestley make her the quickest to feel guilty?
options: To show that guilt depends on willingness to learn, not on the size of the act
Because she is afraid of the police
To make the audience dislike her
questions.explanation: Priestley shows that people can learn. Sheila’s quick shame sets her apart from her parents.

questions.prompt: Which sentence treats Sheila as Priestley’s construct?
options: Through Sheila’s immediate shame, Priestley shows the audience that change is possible.
Sheila feels really bad about what she did.
Sheila should have bought a different dress.
Sheila is a nice girl really.
questions.explanation: The first sentence explains what Priestley does with Sheila. The others treat her as a real person.
questions.misconception: Writing about characters as if they were real people.

questions.prompt: Trace how Sheila learns across the play, and explain what Priestley gains from her change. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley shows Sheila moving from a sheltered, spoilt daughter to the family’s sharpest critic. At the start she calls her mother “Mummy” (Sheila, Act 1) and is delighted with her ring. Once she sees the photograph, she admits her part at once and is ashamed, unlike her father. She then warns Gerald that the Inspector already knows, urges her mother to stop and returns the ring, so each act shows her thinking more independently. Priestley uses her to carry his hope that the younger generation would build a fairer society after the war.
checklist: Traces Sheila’s change across the play
Uses a short, accurate reference
Contrasts her with her father or mother
Uses moments from more than 1 act
Links her change to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Tracing change needs evidence from early and late in the play.

units.title: Sheila: how far does she change?
units.summary: Sheila refuses to let her parents pretend, but Priestley leaves room for doubt about her motives and her future. Take a clear view, then weigh the other reading.

questions.prompt: Early in the play Sheila calls her mother Mummy. What does she call her later, when she begs her to stop?
questions.explanation: AQA’s examiners in 2023 suggested the change may show growing maturity or a new distance between them.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Sheila refuses to let her parents off the hook after the Inspector leaves.
The play shows whether Sheila marries Gerald.
Sheila hands back the ring as her own decision.

questions.explanation: Priestley leaves her future open: the play ends before we see whether she will marry Gerald.

questions.prompt: Who says it is “what he made me feel” (Act 3) that matters, not who the Inspector was?
questions.explanation: Sheila cares about the effect of the evening, not the Inspector’s identity. That is a sign of real change.

questions.prompt: Match each moment to the sign of change in Sheila.
pairs: She admits her part at once and is ashamed
She hands it back as her own decision
She will not let her parents pretend
None yet: she is playful and pleased with her ring
questions.explanation: The opening gives the starting point. Each later moment shows a step forward.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2024 report noted students who saw Sheila as less selfish but still far from selfless. What evidence supports caution?
options: Her first reaction to the Milwards story is partly about how it makes her look.
She refuses to admit her part.
She sides with her parents after the hoax.
She takes the ring back at once.
questions.explanation: Some readers see her shame as guilt about herself as much as grief for Eva. That is a fair point to weigh.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is stronger?
options: Sheila changes more than anyone, although Priestley hints that her guilt is partly about herself.
Sheila could have changed, but it could also mean she did not change at all.
Sheila may or may not change; it is impossible to say.
Sheila changes, and also does not change.
questions.explanation: AQA’s 2023 examiners warned against ‘it could mean this but it could also mean the opposite’. Take a view, then weigh the other reading.
questions.misconception: Offering 2 opposite readings without reaching a judgement.

questions.prompt: What could the change from Mummy to Mother suggest?
options: Growing maturity, or a new distance from her mother
That she has forgotten her mother’s name
That she is angry with her father
questions.explanation: Small changes of address like this are precise evidence for an answer about character development.

questions.prompt: In Act 3 Sheila asks whether anyone has brought the girl back to life. What does the rhetorical question do?
options: It demands an answer her parents cannot give, exposing their relief.
It shows she believes Eva is alive.
It asks the Inspector for information.
questions.explanation: Her rhetorical questions challenge her parents. Whatever the Inspector was, the harm they did remains.

questions.prompt: What is Sheila for, in Priestley’s design?
options: She shows the audience that people can learn, which gives the play its hope.
She explains the plot to the audience.
questions.explanation: She represents the younger generation Priestley trusted to build a fairer post-war Britain.

questions.prompt: How far does Sheila change? Write a paragraph that takes a clear view and weighs the other reading.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Sheila changes more than any other character, although Priestley keeps that change believable by showing its limits. After the Inspector leaves she refuses to let her parents “pretend all over again” (Sheila, Act 3), and she cares about what the evening made her feel rather than whether the Inspector was real. Yet her first reaction at Milwards is partly about how the story makes her look, and the play ends before we know whether she will marry Gerald. Priestley offers the audience hope through Sheila, but leaves her future open, so the work of change is left to them as well.
checklist: States a clear view about how far she changes
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Weighs a counter-reading with evidence
Notes that her future is left open
Links to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: A judgement plus a weighed alternative is what examiners reward on ‘how far’ questions.

units.title: Eric Birling
units.summary: Eric is awkward, drinks too much and treats Eva the most disturbingly, yet he accepts his guilt and turns on his parents. His change is a first step, not a full one.

questions.prompt: What did Eric give Eva when she was pregnant?
options: Money he had stolen from his father’s office
questions.explanation: He tried to help her, but the money was stolen. When she found out where it came from, she refused it.

questions.prompt: Who calls Eric “squiffy” (Act 1)?
questions.explanation: Sheila’s teasing hints at Eric’s drinking, one of the secrets the evening exposes.

questions.prompt: Match each trait to the evidence for it.
pairs: His opening stage direction shows an awkward mix of shyness and confidence
Asks why workers should not try for higher wages
Admits bluntly what the family did to the girl
Tells his father he is not a father to turn to in trouble
questions.explanation: Eric’s traits pull in different directions. Priestley makes him neither hero nor villain.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Eric made Eva pregnant.
Eric kept Eva as his mistress in Morgan Terrace.
Eric met Eva at the Palace bar.
Eric stole money from his father’s office.

questions.explanation: Gerald, not Eric, provided rooms for Daisy. Examiners in 2025 reported answers that confused the 2 young men.

questions.prompt: A student writes that Eric rescued Daisy from Alderman Meggarty. What is wrong?
options: That was Gerald; Eric met Eva later, when he was drunk.
Meggarty is not in the play.
It was Birling who rescued her.
questions.explanation: Eric made Eva pregnant and stole money for her; Gerald kept her as his mistress. Mixing them up costs credit.
questions.misconception: Confusing Eric with Gerald.

questions.prompt: Who says “The money’s not the important thing” (Act 3)?
questions.explanation: Birling cares most about the stolen money. Eric has moved on to what happened to Eva.

questions.prompt: Eric tells his father he is not someone a son could turn to in trouble. What does this expose?
options: The emptiness of Birling’s claim to look after his family
That Birling is a kind father
questions.explanation: Birling claimed a man should look after himself and his family. His own son found no help at home.

questions.prompt: Does Eric change?
options: Yes, but not as fully as Sheila: he accepts responsibility, but his confession is the ugliest.
No, he sides with his father at the end.
Yes, completely, and he becomes the hero.
questions.explanation: He accepts guilt and rejects his parents’ relief, yet Priestley stops the audience simply admiring him. His change is a first step.

questions.prompt: Eric often uses informal words such as ‘chap’. What effect does this have?
options: His speech sounds raw and unrehearsed, refusing to soften what happened.
It makes him sound like a judge.
It shows he is the most educated character.
questions.explanation: Informal, blunt language sets him apart from his father’s speeches and his mother’s formality.

questions.prompt: Explain what Eric adds to Priestley’s picture of the older and younger generations. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses Eric to show that the older generation’s values have failed their own children. Eric drinks heavily, treats Eva disturbingly and steals from his father, so he is no hero. Yet once the truth is out he accepts it bluntly, admitting “we did her in all right” (Eric, Act 3), slang that refuses to soften the guilt. He turns on both parents, telling his father he could never go to him for help. After the hoax he will not join their relief. Priestley places him beside Sheila to show his hope that the young could learn.
checklist: Makes a clear argument about the generations
Acknowledges Eric’s faults
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Shows Eric turning on his parents
Links to Priestley’s hope in the young
questions.explanation: Eric is complicated on purpose. Strong answers keep both his guilt and his change in view.

units.title: Gerald Croft
units.summary: Gerald helped Eva more than anyone and also used her. He is young but sides with the older Birlings, showing that youth alone does not make someone open to change.

questions.prompt: Who are Gerald’s parents?
questions.explanation: His parents are titled and own a larger firm than Birling’s. They are abroad on the night of the dinner.

questions.prompt: Where is Gerald during the Inspector’s final speech?
options: Out of the house, after going for a walk
questions.explanation: He leaves in Act 2 and returns after the Inspector has gone. Missing the speech helps explain why he is quick to believe in a hoax.

questions.prompt: Which details form the case for Gerald?
options: He rescued Daisy from Alderman Meggarty.
He found her somewhere to live and gave her money.
He ended the affair when it suited him.
He kept the affair secret from Sheila.
questions.explanation: The other details belong to the case against. Priestley makes him the most complicated confessor.

questions.prompt: Who says “I hate those hard-eyed dough-faced women” (Act 2) about some of the women at the Palace bar?
questions.explanation: Gerald’s disgust shows that he, too, judges women by their looks and class.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Gerald works hard in Act 3 to prove the Inspector a fraud.
Gerald’s last move is to offer Sheila the ring again.
Gerald accepts full responsibility and sides with Sheila and Eric.

questions.explanation: Gerald leads the effort to explain the evening away. By outlook he belongs with the older Birlings.

questions.prompt: Eduqas’s 2025 report found references to Gerald’s ‘toxic masculinity’ that were often not secure. What is the better approach?
options: Describe what Gerald does and says, and what Priestley shows through it.
Use as many modern labels as possible.
Avoid writing about Gerald at all.
Say he is a typical man.
questions.explanation: Modern labels used loosely weaken an answer. Evidence from the play is stronger.
questions.misconception: Using modern labels loosely instead of evidence.

questions.prompt: Gerald is young, like Sheila and Eric. Why does Priestley place him with the older Birlings?
options: To show that class and self-interest can matter more than age
Because he is secretly older than he looks
Because he is related to Mrs Birling
questions.explanation: Youth alone does not make a person open to change. Gerald has too much to lose.

questions.prompt: Eduqas’s 2025 report praised 2 details in answers about Gerald. Which pair?
options: The ring and his absence from the final speech
His friendship with Edna and his letters
questions.explanation: Small, precise details like these show you know the play well.

questions.prompt: Which sentence treats Gerald as Priestley’s construct?
options: Priestley makes Gerald’s kindness real but self-serving, so the audience sees how even a generous rich man can use a poor woman.
Gerald is quite nice to Daisy at first but then dumps her.
questions.explanation: The first sentence names Priestley and his purpose. The others react to Gerald as if he were real.
questions.misconception: Writing about characters as if they were real people.

questions.prompt: Gerald is young, yet he ends the play on the older Birlings’ side. Explain why Priestley places him there. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley makes Gerald the most sympathetic confessor, but by the end he sides with the older Birlings. He rescued Daisy from Meggarty and gave her somewhere to live, and Sheila respects his honesty. Yet he made her his mistress, ended it when it suited him and hid it from Sheila. He misses the Inspector’s final speech, and on his return he leads the effort to prove a hoax, then offers the ring with “Everything’s all right now, Sheila” (Gerald, Act 3). Priestley uses him to show that class and self-interest can outweigh youth.
checklist: Gives a balanced view of Gerald’s actions
Notes his absence from the final speech
Shows him siding with the older Birlings
Uses a short, accurate quotation
States Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Gerald is a test case for Priestley’s idea about the generations. Strong answers explain why he falls on the older side.

units.title: Eva Smith and Daisy Renton
units.summary: Eva never appears on stage: we know her only through people who harmed her. She is both an individual and a symbol of every working person.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about Eva is true or false.

statements.s: Eva never appears on stage.
Eva helped to lead a strike.
Eva tells her own story in Act 3.

questions.explanation: Everything the audience knows about her comes from others. That silence is part of Priestley’s point.

questions.prompt: Who calls Eva’s a “promising life” (Act 1)?
questions.explanation: The Inspector stresses what was lost. The details the family give show a spirited, principled young woman.

questions.prompt: Match each name to a reading of it.
pairs: Recalls Eve, the first woman in the Bible
One of the commonest English surnames
A common flower, fresh and easily picked
questions.explanation: These are interpretations, not facts Priestley stated. Present them tentatively.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2024 report highlighted an answer about Eva’s voicelessness. What can her silence represent?
options: The people in 1912 who had no vote and no one to speak for them
Priestley forgetting to write her lines
questions.explanation: Keeping her offstage makes the audience notice how little power she had to speak for herself.

questions.prompt: Match what we learn about Eva to who tells us.
pairs: She was a good worker who stood up for the others
She lost her job over a moment’s jealousy
She was grateful and fond of Gerald
She would not take stolen money
questions.explanation: Each account also reveals the teller. Gerald’s, for example, flatters his own kindness.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Priestley named her Daisy because daisies are easily picked.’ What is the problem?
options: It presents an interpretation as a fact Priestley stated.
The student should not mention names.
questions.explanation: Readings of the names can be useful, but say ‘this may suggest’ rather than claiming to know Priestley’s reason.
questions.misconception: Stating interpretations of names as facts.

questions.prompt: In the final speech the Inspector widens Eva into “millions” (Inspector, Act 3). What does this show?
options: She is a symbol of every working person whose life depends on the powerful.
There were millions of girls called Eva.
The Birlings knew millions of workers.
questions.explanation: Eva is both an individual and a symbol. The move from 1 girl to millions widens the play’s message.

questions.prompt: Why might Priestley keep Eva offstage rather than show her?
options: So the audience judges the family by their own accounts, and notices her lack of voice
Because she is not important to the plot
questions.explanation: Writing about what Priestley does with Eva is stronger than writing about her as if she were a real person.

questions.prompt: Almost every account of Eva comes from someone who harmed her. What should this make a careful student do?
options: Treat what they say as claims, since each teller has reasons to tell it their way
Assume the opposite of what they say
questions.explanation: Say what the characters claim. That keeps your answer accurate and shows awareness of how Priestley tells the story.

questions.prompt: Eva never appears on stage. Explain what Priestley achieves by keeping her offstage. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley never lets Eva speak, and that silence is his point. Everything the audience learns comes from the people who harmed her: Birling admits she was a good worker who stood up for others, and Eric reveals that she refused stolen money. These details suggest a principled young woman, yet she has no voice of her own, like the people of 1912 who had no vote and no one to speak for them. In the final speech the Inspector widens her into millions of ordinary working people, so she becomes a symbol of everyone whose life depends on the choices of the powerful.
checklist: Explains the effect of keeping Eva offstage
Uses details from at least 2 accounts
Notes that accounts come from people who harmed her
Explains her symbolic role
Uses relevant context about 1912
questions.explanation: Write about what Priestley does with Eva, not what Eva felt. That keeps the answer accurate and analytical.

units.title: Edna and the world offstage
units.summary: Edna, the maid, is a working-class woman inside the house while the family discuss another they never thought about. Offstage characters show how far the Birlings’ world reaches.

questions.prompt: Which working-class character is seen on stage in the play?
questions.explanation: Edna is the Birlings’ maid. Eva never appears, and the others are offstage figures.

questions.prompt: Match each offstage character to what they add.
pairs: Titled parents abroad on the night of the dinner
A respected councillor who preys on young women
Confirms that no Inspector Goole is on the force
Gerald’s friend, whose rooms Daisy lives in
questions.explanation: Offstage characters make Brumley feel real and show how far the Birlings’ influence reaches.

questions.prompt: Where are the rooms that Gerald arranged for Daisy?
questions.explanation: They belonged to Gerald’s friend Charlie Brunswick, who was away.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Edna is on stage in the opening moments, clearing the table.
Edna has many long speeches.
Birling telephones the Chief Constable in Act 3.

questions.explanation: Edna has very few lines. Birling’s call to the Chief Constable shows the powerful looking after each other.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley keep so many important people offstage?
options: To remind the audience of the whole society around the Birlings
Because the stage was too small
Because they have no effect on the plot
questions.explanation: The play takes place in 1 room but is about a whole town: powerful friends who protect the family, and unseen workers whose lives they shape.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2025 report praised students writing about Edna, but warned against one approach. Which?
options: Describing her treatment emotively without evidence from the play
Mentioning that she is a maid
Noticing that she opens the door
questions.explanation: Claims about Edna must be tied to what happens on stage. Emotive guesses about her life earn little.
questions.misconception: Describing a minor character emotively without evidence.

questions.prompt: Birling telephones the Chief Constable to check on the Inspector. What does this suggest?
options: The powerful look after each other.
The Chief Constable is the Inspector.
questions.explanation: Priestley shows a network of wealthy men that keeps each other safe, while girls like Eva have no one.

questions.prompt: The current touring production shows Sheila and Edna leaving together at the end. How should a student use this?
options: Name the production and link it to the script, since it is a staging choice, not Priestley’s text
Quote it as a line from the play
questions.explanation: A production can support a point, but you must say which one and tie it back to what Priestley wrote.
questions.misconception: Treating a director’s staging as Priestley’s text.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses Edna most effectively in an answer on class?
options: Priestley opens with Edna clearing the table, so a working-class woman is on stage before Eva is ever mentioned, and the family barely notice her.
Edna is the maid and she is poor, which is sad.
questions.explanation: The first sentence turns a staging detail into evidence for an idea. The others state facts without saying why they matter.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley uses a minor or offstage character to widen the play beyond 1 room. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Alderman Meggarty never appears, yet Priestley uses him to expose the world the Birlings belong to. Gerald describes “a notorious womaniser” (Gerald, Act 2) who pesters young women at the Palace bar, but Meggarty is still a respected councillor in Brumley. His reputation is protected in the same way that Birling expects the Chief Constable to protect him. Through an offstage figure, Priestley shows a network of powerful men who keep each other safe, while a woman like Eva has no one to protect her.
checklist: Chooses a minor or offstage character
Uses accurate detail about them
Links them to a wider idea such as class or power
Explains what they show about the Birlings’ world
Keeps the focus on Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Pearson’s 2025 report credited answers on minor characters. A sentence or 2 can show you know the whole play.

units.title: Responsibility
units.summary: The play is an argument between Birling’s view that a man need only look after himself and the Inspector’s view that we are responsible for each other. The confessions and the ending test which is right.

questions.prompt: Which character accepts responsibility at once, and holds on to it after the hoax?
questions.explanation: Sheila admits her part as soon as she sees the photograph and refuses to pretend in Act 3.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Birling refuses any responsibility for sacking Eva.
Mrs Birling blames the father of the child.
Gerald accepts full responsibility and rejects the hoax.
Eric turns on his parents for refusing responsibility.

questions.explanation: Gerald is sorry but seizes on the hoax. The characters split according to whether they accept their part.

questions.prompt: Match each character to how far they accept responsibility.
pairs: Yes, at once, and keeps hold of it after the hoax
Yes, and turns on his parents for refusing
Partly: sorry, but quick to seize on the hoax
No: she blames the father, then the girl
questions.explanation: This split is the backbone of most answers on responsibility. Organise by who accepts and who refuses.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between personal and social responsibility in the play?
options: Personal is owning up to what you did; social is caring about people you may never meet.
Personal is about money; social is about parties.
They mean exactly the same thing.
Personal is the Inspector’s idea; social is Birling’s.
questions.explanation: Sheila and Eric learn the first. The Inspector wants the audience to learn the second.

questions.prompt: Who tells Gerald and Eric that “a man has to make his own way” (Act 1)?
questions.explanation: Birling’s Act 1 speech sets out the selfish view that the Inspector answers in Act 3. Everything in between tests which view is right.

questions.prompt: Why does the idea of a chain of events let each character claim innocence?
options: None of the 5 actions killed Eva alone.
questions.explanation: Because no single act was fatal, each can say it was not their fault. The Inspector insists the guilt is shared.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2020 report found one approach kept responsibility answers at a low level. Which?
options: Listing each character’s crime in turn
questions.explanation: Organise by idea, for example who accepts guilt and who refuses it, and use characters as evidence.
questions.misconception: Listing characters one by one on a theme question.

questions.prompt: How does the welfare-state debate of 1945 connect to the theme of responsibility?
options: A welfare state is responsibility shared by everyone through taxes and public services.
It has no connection to the play.
It made charities like Mrs Birling’s more powerful.
It meant employers like Birling could not be sacked.
questions.explanation: The Birlings stand for the old idea that the comfortable owe nothing to the poor. The Inspector speaks for the new one.

questions.prompt: How does the ending test the characters’ responsibility?
options: The older characters shake off responsibility, then the telephone call brings it back.
The Inspector returns to arrest them.
It shows responsibility does not matter.
questions.explanation: Sheila and Eric have already accepted their guilt, so the call confirms what they know. The others are caught out.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley builds the whole play as an argument about responsibility. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley frames the play as an argument about responsibility. In Act 1 Birling tells the young men that a man need only look after himself and his family; in Act 3 the Inspector answers that everyone is responsible for everyone else. The confessions in between show “a chain of events” (Inspector, Act 1) in which no single act killed Eva, so each character can claim innocence, yet together they destroyed her. The ending sorts the characters: Sheila and Eric hold on to their guilt, while the older Birlings and Gerald try to shake it off, and the telephone call brings it back. For an audience debating a welfare state in 1945, the lesson was clear.
checklist: Uses the 2 framing speeches
Explains the chain of events idea
Organises by who accepts and who refuses
Uses the ending as evidence
Links to 1945 context
questions.explanation: Build the answer around ideas, not a list of characters.

units.title: Class: capital and labour
units.summary: Birling is a capitalist who puts profit first and sees workers as a threat. Priestley gives the workers’ case to Eric, Sheila and the Inspector.

questions.prompt: What is capitalism?
options: Private owners run businesses for profit, and each person looks after their own interests.
The community shares responsibility for everyone.
questions.explanation: Birling owns the means of production and profits from other people’s work. He is Priestley’s portrait of a capitalist.

questions.prompt: What is socialism, as Priestley understood it?
options: The community shares responsibility for everyone, and wealth is shared more fairly.
Each person looks after only themselves.
questions.explanation: Priestley was a socialist. The Inspector’s final speech sets out that view in plain terms.

questions.prompt: Who asks “Why shouldn’t they try for higher wages?” (Act 1)
questions.explanation: Eric takes the workers’ side against his father in Act 1. It is an early sign of the split between the generations.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their view of workers.
pairs: They are a threat that must be kept down
Owners who push up prices cannot blame workers for pushing up wages
Workers are people, not cheap labour
It is better that people ask than take
questions.explanation: Priestley gives Birling’s view to 1 character and the workers’ case to 3 others. The play becomes a debate Birling loses.

questions.prompt: Eric’s full line balances the workers’ wages against the owners’ prices. What does this balance expose?
options: A double standard: owners who push prices up call workers greedy for pushing wages up
That Eric wants to run the factory
That prices and wages are always equal
questions.explanation: The balanced sentence makes the unfairness obvious. Priestley lets the son see what the father will not.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Birling refuses the strikers’ demand for higher wages.
He sacks the leaders of the strike.
He later agrees to the rise and rehires Eva.
The Inspector reminds Birling that public men have responsibilities.

questions.explanation: Birling never gives way. The Inspector’s reply challenges the idea that status puts him above judgement.

questions.prompt: A student writes that the strikers earned nothing at all. What is the problem?
options: The play gives no such figure; be precise and never invent wages.
The strikers were paid very well.
There was no strike in the play.
questions.explanation: Birling says the rise would have added about 12% to his labour costs. Avoid vague or invented claims.
questions.misconception: Inventing figures the play does not give.

questions.prompt: Birling warns that if employers are not tough, workers will soon be “asking for the earth” (Birling, Act 1). What does this show?
options: He sees workers as a threat to be controlled.
He wants to give workers land.
questions.explanation: Workers appear to him as a danger, not as people. The Inspector later turns the phrase back on him.

questions.prompt: Why is Eva’s first dismissal so important to Priestley’s argument?
options: She is sacked for asking for a fair wage, and every later stage of her decline follows from it.
It is the only thing that happens to her.
questions.explanation: For a worker in 1912, standing up for yourself could cost everything. The first link sets the chain moving.

questions.prompt: Explain how Birling’s treatment of his workers serves Priestley’s attack on capitalism. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley presents Birling as a man who values profit above people. Even at his daughter’s engagement he toasts a merger with the Crofts “for lower costs and higher prices” (Birling, Act 1), and when his workers strike for higher wages he sacks the leaders, calling it his duty to keep costs down. Priestley sets this view against Eric, Sheila and the Inspector, who insist that workers are people, so the play becomes an argument that Birling loses. For an audience that had just voted for a fairer society in 1945, Birling stood for the old order they were rejecting.
checklist: Makes a clear argument about capitalism
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Refers to the strike and the sacking
Shows how other characters answer Birling
Links to the 1945 audience
questions.explanation: Strong answers treat Birling as Priestley’s example of a system, not just a bad boss.

units.title: Class: status, snobbery and charity
units.summary: Class is about rank as well as money. Birling climbs the ladder, Mrs Birling judges Eva by class, and the powerful protect each other.

questions.prompt: Which family ranks above the Birlings?
questions.explanation: Birling admits Crofts Limited is older and bigger than his firm. The engagement is a step up for his family.

questions.prompt: Match each class to the characters who belong to it.
pairs: Sir George and Lady Croft; Gerald
questions.explanation: Mrs Birling married down, and Birling hopes to rise through Sheila’s marriage. Class shapes every relationship in the play.

questions.prompt: Who reminds the Inspector “I was an alderman for years” (Act 1)?
questions.explanation: Birling expects rank to protect him. The Inspector is not impressed.

questions.prompt: Mrs Birling refers to working girls as a group rather than as people. What does this show?
options: She judges Eva by class before she knows anything else about her.
She has met many working girls.
She wants to help them all.
questions.explanation: Treating a person as a category means nothing the girl says can be believed.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Birling telephones the Chief Constable to check on the Inspector.
The town treats Alderman Meggarty as respectable.
The Inspector is impressed by Birling’s rank.

questions.explanation: Priestley shows a network of wealthy men that keeps each other safe, and an Inspector who will not bow to it.

questions.prompt: The Inspector tells Birling that public men “have responsibilities as well as privileges” (Inspector, Act 2). What does this challenge?
options: The idea that status puts people above judgement
The idea that workers should strike
The idea that charity is good
The idea that the Titanic is unsinkable
questions.explanation: Birling expects his position to protect him. The Inspector insists that position brings duties too.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Class is just about how much money you have.’ Which detail proves this wrong?
options: Birling is rich, but he knows the Crofts rank above him.
questions.explanation: Birling’s wealth is new money. Titled families like the Crofts still rank higher, which is why the marriage matters to him.
questions.misconception: Treating class as money alone.

questions.prompt: Why should a class answer show that Priestley attacks a whole system, not just 1 or 2 bad people?
options: The shop, the factory, the charity and the marriage all work for the wealthy.
Because only Birling is to blame.
Because examiners want a list of characters.
Because the play has no villains.
questions.explanation: Priestley shows the same pattern in every institution Eva meets. That is a conceptual argument about class.

questions.prompt: After the Inspector leaves, what is Birling’s first worry?
questions.explanation: His reputation matters more than the girl. Priestley shows status as the thing Birling values most.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley shows class working as a system rather than as a few bad individuals. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley shows class as a system that protects the powerful and silences the poor. Birling is rich, yet he still measures himself against the titled Crofts and hopes a knighthood will lift him higher. Mrs Birling, her husband’s “social superior” (stage direction, Act 1), uses her place on a charity committee to decide who deserves help, and judges Eva by her class before hearing her story. Meanwhile the Chief Constable and Alderman Meggarty show a network of respectable men who keep each other safe. Priestley uses the Birlings’ snobbery to persuade his 1945 audience that such a system should end.
checklist: Argues that class is a system
Discusses rank as well as money
Uses Mrs Birling’s charity as evidence
Uses a short, accurate reference
Links to Priestley’s purpose in 1945
questions.explanation: A conceptual answer shows class working through several institutions at once.

units.title: Gender: women’s lives
units.summary: In 1912 women had no vote and working-class women had few jobs. Priestley shows women of every class hemmed in by decisions others make for them.

questions.prompt: Could any woman vote in a general election in 1912?
questions.explanation: Women over 30 who met a property qualification gained the vote in 1918. In 1912 no woman could vote in a general election.

questions.prompt: Put Eva’s situations in the order they happen.
items: Factory worker
Shop assistant
With no job, dependent on men
questions.explanation: Each step leaves her with less control over her life. Priestley shows how few choices a working-class woman had.

questions.prompt: Where does Mrs Birling have power?
options: Only in the limited areas open to women of her class, such as the household and a charity
questions.explanation: She uses that limited power to keep other women in their place.

questions.prompt: Match each attitude to the right description.
pairs: Challenges Gerald and returns the ring
Accepts that men behave badly and says nothing
questions.explanation: The 2 women stand for 2 generations. Priestley shows 1 learning and 1 refusing.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2023 examiners praised answers that linked women’s lack of a vote to who is allowed to speak in the play. Which detail fits?
options: Eva never speaks and Edna has only a handful of lines.
Women give all the long speeches.
questions.explanation: Meanwhile Sheila speaks with more and more authority. Voice becomes a way of writing about power.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Sheila is treated as a child at the start of the play.
Sheila’s engagement matters to her father partly for business.
Sheila never challenges her parents.

questions.explanation: As the play goes on she returns the ring and challenges her parents. Her life is safe but limited at first.

questions.prompt: Which use of context would AQA’s 2020 report criticise in an answer on women?
options: A list of facts about suffragettes with no link to the play
1 short point about the vote, used to sharpen a comment on Eva’s silence
A note that Sheila could not vote, linked to her lack of power
A link between the 1945 audience and Sheila’s change
questions.explanation: Use 1 short contextual point to sharpen a comment on a moment. Lists of facts earn little.
questions.misconception: Listing facts about the period with no link to the play.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley make Sheila’s engagement matter to Birling for business reasons?
options: To show that even a wealthy woman’s life was shaped by men’s plans
To show Sheila runs the business
questions.explanation: Sheila is expected to marry well. Priestley shows women of every class hemmed in by others’ decisions.

questions.prompt: Which sentence links gender to class most effectively?
options: Eva is exploited as a worker and as a woman, so Priestley shows class and gender working together against her.
Women had a hard time in the past.
Sheila is a girl and Eva is a girl.
questions.explanation: Linking class and gender makes an answer more conceptual.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley shows women of different classes hemmed in by other people’s decisions. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley shows women of every class hemmed in by decisions that others make for them. Eva loses her place at the factory and then at Milwards, each time at the hands of someone more powerful, until she depends on men. Sheila’s life is safe but limited: she calls her mother “Mummy” (Sheila, Act 1) and her marriage matters to her father as a business link. Mrs Birling has power only within a charity, and uses it against another woman. In 1912 none of them could vote, and Priestley lets the audience see how little control they had, while Sheila’s growing confidence points to change.
checklist: Covers women of more than 1 class
Uses a short, accurate reference
Shows how others decide women’s lives
Uses 1912 context such as the vote
Notes Sheila’s change
questions.explanation: A strong answer compares women across classes and links their situation to Priestley’s purpose.

units.title: Gender: men’s attitudes to women
units.summary: Every man in the Birling circle uses his power over women, and their behaviour is excused while women are judged. Sheila answers back.

questions.prompt: How does Gerald describe the other women at the Palace bar?
questions.explanation: His disgust shows that he judges women by their looks and class, even while presenting himself as a rescuer.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Alderman Meggarty is still a respected figure in Brumley.
The older Birlings want Gerald’s affair hushed up.
Eva is offered help because she is pregnant.

questions.explanation: Eva, pregnant and unmarried, is refused help. The double standard punishes women for what men do.

questions.prompt: Match each man to his power over women.
pairs: Sacks Eva and expects Sheila to marry to suit the business
Keeps Daisy as his mistress, then ends it
Pressures Eva into letting him into her lodgings when drunk
Preys on young women at the Palace bar
questions.explanation: Whether as employer or as lover, each man uses his power. Priestley shows a pattern, not a single villain.

questions.prompt: Who mocks Gerald’s story of rescue by calling him a “fairy prince” (Act 2)?
questions.explanation: The sarcastic fairy-tale image shows Sheila refusing the role of grateful woman.

questions.prompt: What double standard does Priestley expose?
options: Men’s behaviour is excused while women are judged for it.
Women are paid more than men.
Men are punished more harshly than women.
questions.explanation: Gerald’s affair is something to hush up; Eva is refused help. The same behaviour lands differently on men and women.

questions.prompt: Gerald condemns Meggarty for preying on young women. What is ironic about this?
options: Gerald does not see his own part in using Daisy.
questions.explanation: He judges another man while telling a story in which he keeps a mistress.

questions.prompt: A student writes about Eva only as a victim of men. What is missing?
options: She is exploited as a worker as well as a woman.
Nothing: she has no other role.
questions.explanation: Birling and Milwards exploit her as a worker; Gerald and Eric as a woman. Linking the 2 makes the answer more conceptual.
questions.misconception: Separating gender from class when writing about Eva.

questions.prompt: By 1945 women had the vote on equal terms and had done vital war work. How might this shape the audience’s response?
options: They could see how much had changed since 1912, and how much still needed to.
They would approve of the men’s behaviour.
They would not notice the men’s attitudes.
They would think the play was set in 1945.
questions.explanation: Priestley shows the men’s attitudes as part of the same selfish system as Birling’s treatment of workers.

questions.prompt: Eric admits that “a chap easily turns nasty” (Eric, Act 3) when he has been drinking. What does Priestley show by giving this admission to a wealthy young man?
options: That money and freedom without guidance let men treat working-class women as something to take
That drinking was against the law
That Eric is proud of what he did
questions.explanation: Priestley presents Eric’s behaviour as the most disturbing, and as part of a pattern of male power.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley exposes a pattern in the way the male characters treat women. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley shows that every man in the Birling circle uses his power over women. Gerald rescues Daisy but makes her his mistress, and he speaks of other women in the Palace bar with open disgust: “I hate those hard-eyed dough-faced women” (Gerald, Act 2). Eric pressures Eva into letting him into her lodgings, and Meggarty preys on young women while remaining respectable. Their behaviour is excused or hushed up, while Eva, pregnant and unmarried, is refused help. Sheila’s sarcasm exposes the pattern, and Priestley lets her answer back in a way Eva never could.
checklist: Covers more than 1 man
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains the double standard
Notes Sheila answering back
Writes about Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Show a pattern across the male characters rather than a list of separate crimes.

units.title: Age and the generations
units.summary: The Inspector’s questions split the family by age: the older Birlings defend themselves, while Sheila and Eric change. Gerald is young but sides with the old.

questions.prompt: Which characters belong to the younger generation that changes?
questions.explanation: Gerald is young but sides with the older Birlings. Youth alone does not make a character change.
questions.misconception: Assuming every young character changes.

questions.prompt: Where does Gerald fit in the generational split?
options: He is young, but sides with the older Birlings.
questions.explanation: He leads the effort to prove a hoax and offers the ring as if nothing has happened.

questions.prompt: Who sneers at “the famous younger generation who know it all” (Act 3)?
questions.explanation: Birling mocks his children just before the telephone proves them right.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the comparison to the right generation.
pairs: Deny, blame others and worry about reputation
Accept guilt and feel for Eva
questions.explanation: The split is clearest after the Inspector has gone, when each side shows what it really values.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Mrs Birling calls Sheila childish when she pleads with her.
Eric confronts both parents about how they treated Eva.
Birling praises his children for their honesty in Act 3.

questions.explanation: Birling mocks the young, and the telephone call then proves them right.

questions.prompt: Why is Birling’s sarcasm about the younger generation ironic?
options: The telephone call moments later proves the young right.
questions.explanation: The final irony of the play falls on Birling, caught mocking the very people who understood.

questions.prompt: AQA set a question on how older and younger characters respond to the Inspector in 2023. What advice from the guide matters most?
options: Trace the responses across the whole play, including after the Inspector has gone.
Discuss Gerald as a member of the younger generation that changes.
questions.explanation: The split is clearest once the Inspector has left, when the hoax lets each character choose.

questions.prompt: Why did Priestley give the hope of change to the young?
options: He believed the young could build a better society after the war.
The young were in charge in 1912.
Young people bought most theatre tickets.
questions.explanation: The older characters hold on to the attitudes of 1912; Sheila and Eric carry the hope of 1945.

questions.prompt: Which sentence explains the generational split as Priestley’s choice?
options: Priestley splits the family by age so that his 1945 audience sees the young learning while the old cling to the past.
The parents are old and boring and the children are young and fun.
Sheila and Eric are nicer than their parents.
Everyone argues because families always argue.
questions.explanation: The first sentence names Priestley, a method and an effect on the audience.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley divides the family by age, and what he wants his audience to take from the split. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley splits the family by age to show his hope in the young. When the Inspector questions them, the older Birlings deny and blame, while Sheila and Eric feel guilt. The split becomes open conflict once the hoax seems proved: Sheila warns that her parents are ready to “pretend all over again” (Sheila, Act 3), while Birling mocks his children. Gerald, though young, joins the older side, which shows that class and self-interest can outweigh age. For a 1945 audience, many hoping the post-war generation would build a fairer country, the young offered the way forward.
checklist: Contrasts older and younger responses
Uses moments after the Inspector leaves
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains where Gerald fits
Links to Priestley’s hope in 1945
questions.explanation: The strongest answers trace the split to the very end of the play.

units.title: Time
units.summary: Priestley sets the play in 1912 so a 1945 audience can judge it with hindsight. The action is continuous, and the ending sends the family back to the start.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the play’s action is continuous?
options: The 3 acts follow on without a break in time, in 1 room.
The action jumps forward 2 years in each act.
The actors never leave the stage.
questions.explanation: The audience lives through the evening at the same pace as the family, so the pressure never lets up.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: War came in 1914 and again in 1939.
The Birlings know the Titanic will sink.
The audience of 1945 knows more than the characters about the future.

questions.explanation: This gap between what the audience knows and what the characters know is the source of the play’s dramatic irony.

questions.prompt: Why does Birling’s praise of the Titanic sound foolish to the audience?
options: They know it sank in April 1912.
Birling is talking about a different ship.
They have never heard of it.
questions.explanation: Hindsight turns Birling’s confidence into dramatic irony and makes the audience doubt everything else he says.

questions.prompt: Match each use of time to its effect.
pairs: Hindsight turns Birling’s confidence into irony
The warning in the final speech
It sounds like prophecy to people who lived through the wars
questions.explanation: Time works at several levels in the play. Linking each device to its effect is the key skill.

questions.prompt: Who accuses her parents of behaving as if “nothing much has happened” (Act 3)?
questions.explanation: Sheila refuses to let time wipe the evening away, while her parents want to go back to how things were.

questions.prompt: A student writes that Priestley based the ending on a particular theorist’s book. What is safer?
options: Say Priestley was interested in theories of time; the detail is not needed.
Say the ending has nothing to do with time.
questions.explanation: The guide could not confirm a named source. Saying he was interested in theories of time is accurate and enough.
questions.misconception: Claiming a named theorist as a proven source.

questions.prompt: The ending leaves the audience unsure whether they have watched a warning or been given a second chance. Why might Priestley want this?
options: The audience must decide how to act, as the Birlings must.
He could not decide how to end it.
To make the audience leave early.
questions.explanation: The circular ending suggests the lesson will keep returning until it is learned.

questions.prompt: Gerald offers the ring again as if the evening can be undone. How does the play respond?
options: The telephone rings and the story begins again.
questions.explanation: Gerald wants time to go back to the start of the evening. The play refuses to let it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence links time to Priestley’s purpose most clearly?
options: Writing in 1945 about 1912, Priestley lets his audience see what Birling cannot, so they learn to reject his confidence.
The play is set a long time ago.
Time is a theme in the play.
The clock on the wall shows the time.
questions.explanation: Naming both dates and explaining the effect is a neat way into time and dramatic irony.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley uses the gap between 1912 and 1945, and the ending, to shape the audience’s response. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley sets the play in 1912 so that his 1945 audience can judge it with hindsight. They know that the Titanic sank and that war followed in 1914 and again in 1939, so Birling’s confidence becomes dramatic irony, and the Inspector’s warning of “fire and blood and anguish” (Inspector, Act 3) sounds like prophecy. The continuous action keeps the pressure on, and the ending sends the family back to the start of their ordeal with a single telephone call. Priestley suggests that time will keep repeating the lesson until it is learned, which leaves his own audience with a choice.
checklist: Explains the 1912 and 1945 dates and the hindsight
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Comments on continuous action
Explains the circular ending
Links to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Time questions reward answers that connect the setting and the ending to Priestley’s purpose.

units.title: Morality and the law, secrets and selfishness
units.summary: Almost nothing the Birlings did was against the law: the Inspector judges them by a moral standard. Every character also hides something and puts their own comfort first.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the law in 1912 is true or false.

statements.s: Birling broke the law by sacking the strike leaders.
Sheila broke the law by having Eva dismissed.
Eric broke the law by stealing money from the office.
Mrs Birling’s committee broke the law by refusing help.

questions.explanation: Only Eric’s theft is clearly a crime. The Inspector condemns the others on moral grounds.

questions.prompt: What standard does the Inspector judge the family by?
options: A moral standard: how they treated another human being
questions.explanation: Pearson’s 2019 report noted answers that saw him as a moral rather than a legal figure.

questions.prompt: Match each action to why the Inspector condemns it.
pairs: He puts profit before a worker’s life
She uses her power out of jealousy
Gerald keeps Daisy as his mistress
He uses her and lets her go
questions.explanation: None of these was a crime, yet each did real harm. That gap is the theme.

questions.prompt: Birling is a magistrate and a friend of the Chief Constable. What does Priestley suggest?
questions.explanation: The moral law of the Inspector’s final speech applies to everyone equally, unlike the law Birling expects to protect him.

questions.prompt: The Inspector says “If there’s nothing else, we’ll have to share our guilt” (Inspector, Act 2). What kind of guilt does he mean?
options: Moral guilt, which no court would convict them of
Guilt that belongs only to Eric
questions.explanation: No court would convict the family, but the Inspector insists they carry the guilt together.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2025 report found that weaker answers on secrets did one thing. What?
questions.explanation: Stronger answers linked secrets to the structure, as revelation follows revelation, and to Priestley’s message.
questions.misconception: Listing each character’s secret without analysis.

questions.prompt: Match each character to what they put first.
questions.explanation: Each confession shows selfishness of a different kind. Pearson’s 2024 report credited answers that linked this to Priestley’s attack on capitalism.

questions.prompt: An Edexcel question on selfishness opens with a quotation from Sheila. What did Pearson’s 2024 report warn against?
options: Discussing only Sheila because the quotation came from her
questions.explanation: Use the quotation as a way in to the whole play.

questions.prompt: Why does Birling care so much about keeping the evening secret?
options: His reputation is everything to him.
He wants to protect Eva’s family.
He wants the Inspector to be promoted.
questions.explanation: He worries about scandal and his knighthood. A society built on hiding things cannot be fair, Priestley suggests.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between what is legal and what is right in the play. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley separates the law from morality. Almost nothing the Birlings did was illegal: an employer could sack a striker, a customer could complain and a charity could refuse help. Only Eric’s theft was clearly a crime. The Inspector therefore judges them by a moral standard, how they treated another human being, and he never arrests anyone. Meanwhile Birling, a magistrate with friends in the police, expects the law to protect him. Priestley shows the law serving the powerful, and sets against it a moral law that applies to everyone equally.
checklist: Explains that most actions were legal
Identifies Eric’s theft as the clear crime
Explains the Inspector’s moral standard
Notes the law serving the powerful
States Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: The gap between legal and right is the heart of this theme. Name it clearly and support it.

units.title: What kind of play is it?
units.summary: The play borrows from the well-made play, the crime thriller and the morality play. Priestley raises each expectation and then breaks it.

questions.prompt: What word describes a play that sets out to teach a lesson?
questions.explanation: A didactic play is designed to teach. Priestley puts a moral lesson inside a gripping story.

questions.prompt: Match each form to what its audience expects.
pairs: A single culprit, exposed and punished
A believable family in a believable room
questions.explanation: Knowing the expectation lets you explain the effect when Priestley breaks it.

questions.prompt: When were morality plays popular?
questions.explanation: They taught right from wrong, often through characters who stood for sins and virtues. The well-made play belongs to the 19th century.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley break the pattern of the well-made play?
options: Order returns for a few minutes, then the telephone breaks it again.
questions.explanation: The well-made play usually ends with order restored. Priestley refuses the tidy ending.

questions.prompt: The critic Benedict Nightingale matched characters to deadly sins. Match each character to the sin he gave them.
questions.explanation: He gave Eric lust, gluttony and sloth. The reading is quoted in the National Theatre’s teacher pack.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley change the usual answer to ‘who did it?’ in a crime thriller?
options: Every suspect played a part, and no one is arrested.
questions.explanation: The disturbing answer is that everyone is guilty. That turns a thriller into a lesson about shared responsibility.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The play is a morality play.’ What should come next for AO2 credit?
options: What Priestley gains from the form, such as offering characters the chance to repent
A list of other morality plays
Nothing: naming the form is enough
questions.explanation: Name the form, then explain its effect. Naming alone is feature-spotting.
questions.misconception: Naming a form without explaining its effect.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley mix an entertaining form with a moral lesson?
options: The audience is gripped by the story and taught how to judge it almost without noticing.
Because he could not choose 1 form.
questions.explanation: Suspense keeps the audience watching while the play does its teaching.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each definition is true or false.

statements.s: A climax is the point of highest tension.
A denouement is the opening scene of a play.
A genre is a type of writing with recognisable features.

questions.explanation: The denouement is the final unravelling of a plot. Using these terms accurately helps AO2.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley uses a form or genre to create an effect. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: The play follows the pattern of a well-made play until the last moment. Secrets come out one by one, each more shocking than the last, and when Gerald’s news and the Infirmary call seem to prove a hoax, order appears to be restored. Then the telephone rings. By denying the audience the comfort of order restored, Priestley makes the lesson impossible to escape: the family must face it again, and so must the audience. The familiar form lulls the audience before the ending unsettles them.
checklist: Names a form accurately
Explains what the audience expects from it
Shows how Priestley follows and then breaks the pattern
Explains the effect on the audience
Links the effect to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Analysis of form means showing what the form makes the audience expect, and what happens when that expectation breaks.

units.title: Stage directions and setting
units.summary: The whole play happens in the Birlings’ dining room, a room built to show off wealth. Stage directions are Priestley’s words too, so you can quote and analyse them.

questions.prompt: Where does the whole play take place?
questions.explanation: Keeping the action in 1 room gives a closed, pressured atmosphere. The Inspector brings the outside world in.

questions.prompt: Which character does the stage direction “easy well-bred young man-about-town” (stage direction, Act 1) describe?
questions.explanation: The direction presents Gerald as confident, upper class and at home in the world of bars.

questions.prompt: Match each character to what their opening stage direction suggests.
pairs: Higher in class than her husband
Uneasy and awkward, hinting at a secret
Authority that does not depend on size or rank
questions.explanation: All 4 descriptions come from the stage directions in Act 1. Each gives the audience a key to the character.

questions.prompt: At the start the table is being cleared of champagne glasses and set with port and cigars. What do these props suggest?
options: A family at ease with its wealth, moments before the Inspector arrives
questions.explanation: The props of a celebration set up the comfort that the Inspector will break.

questions.prompt: Priestley describes the room as “heavily comfortable” (stage direction, Act 1) but “not cosy and homelike” (stage direction, Act 1). What does the contrast suggest?
options: The family has money but lacks warmth and care for others.
The room is cold because the fire is out.
The family has just moved in.
The room belongs to the Crofts.
questions.explanation: The first phrase suggests wealth that weighs the room down; the second takes away any warmth.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Stage directions can be quoted and analysed as Priestley’s words.
All 4 character descriptions quoted in the guide are from Act 3.
At the end of Act 2 the directions track Mrs Birling’s confidence turning to understanding.

questions.explanation: The character descriptions are from Act 1. Directions for how lines are spoken show Priestley controlling pace and response.

questions.prompt: A student writes about ‘the reader’ throughout an essay on the play. What is the better word?
options: The audience, thinking about what they see and hear on stage
questions.explanation: An Inspector Calls is a play. Write about the audience and about lighting, sound, movement and silence.
questions.misconception: Writing about the reader instead of the audience.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2023 examiners praised answers that treated the room in a particular way. Which?
options: As a small model of the Birlings’ class, expensive and shut off from the outside world
questions.explanation: Sheila warns her mother against building a wall between the family and the girl, and the room itself is that wall.

questions.prompt: At the end of Act 2, Priestley’s directions follow Mrs Birling from triumphant demands to sudden understanding. What does this control?
options: The pace and the audience’s response to the dramatic irony
questions.explanation: Directions for delivery let Priestley shape the moment the irony lands.

questions.prompt: Analyse 1 stage direction from Act 1 and explain what it shows the audience. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley describes the Inspector as creating “an impression of massiveness, solidity and purposefulness” (stage direction, Act 1). The direction speaks of an impression rather than size, so his authority comes from presence, not rank or bulk. The 3 nouns suggest weight and determination, in contrast to the light, comfortable family around the table. Before he has said much, the audience sees that this visitor will not be pushed aside, which prepares them for an Inspector who controls the questioning and refuses to be impressed by Birling’s position.
checklist: Quotes a stage direction accurately and labels it
Analyses specific words
Explains what the audience sees
Links the direction to the character’s role
Connects to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Stage directions reward the same close reading as dialogue. Say they are directions and think about the stage picture.

units.title: Lighting, sound and props
units.summary: Soft pink lighting turns harsher when the Inspector arrives, and sounds break in at the worst moments for the family. Lighting, sound and props are methods you can analyse like dialogue.

questions.prompt: What happens to the lighting when the Inspector enters?
questions.explanation: The change is like a spotlight being turned on the family. Pearson’s 2019 report noted many students referred to it.

questions.prompt: Match each sound to the moment it breaks in.
pairs: During Birling’s speech about looking after yourself
At the end of Act 2, as the family realise who the father is
At the very end, as the older characters are laughing
questions.explanation: Each sound arrives at the worst possible moment for the Birlings.

questions.prompt: Put the ring’s movements through the play in order.
items: Gerald gives it to Sheila
Sheila hands it back
Gerald offers it again
Sheila will not take it yet
questions.explanation: Given in Act 1, returned in Act 2 and offered again in Act 3. The ring traces the play’s circular structure.

questions.prompt: The opening lighting is “pink and intimate” (stage direction, Act 1). What does it suggest?
options: The family’s comfortable, flattering view of itself
questions.explanation: Warm, private lighting suits a family who think the outside world cannot touch them.

questions.prompt: The photograph does 2 jobs. What are they?
options: It drives the questioning, and it gives the older characters a loophole later.
It proves Eva is alive and Goole is real.
It decorates the room and shows Eva’s family.
It shows the Titanic and the war.
questions.explanation: Each person looks alone, so each confession is private first. That method plants Gerald’s doubt in Act 3.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The doorbell interrupts Birling’s speech about looking after yourself.
The whole family looks at the photograph together.
The telephone brings news that seems to confirm the hoax, then news that destroys it.

questions.explanation: The photograph is shown 1 at a time. The telephone is used twice in Act 3 with opposite effects.

questions.prompt: Eduqas’s 2025 report praised answers that read the ring as a symbol. What does treating it only as an object miss?
options: It marks the families joining, Sheila’s independence and the play’s circular structure.
It shows the Birlings are poor.
It is a clue to Eva’s identity.
questions.explanation: A prop that is given, returned and offered again carries the story of the engagement and of Sheila’s change.
questions.misconception: Treating props as objects rather than symbols.

questions.prompt: Which sentence links a staging choice to meaning most effectively?
options: The harsh new lighting that comes with the Inspector suggests that the family’s comfortable self-image is about to be exposed.
The lighting changes when the Inspector comes in.
There is lighting in the play.
Priestley uses lighting and sound and props.
questions.explanation: Say what the audience sees, when it happens and what it suggests, in 1 sentence.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley make the final telephone ring just as the older characters are laughing?
options: It catches them at the moment they think they are safe.
To give the actors a cue to bow.
questions.explanation: The timing punishes their relief and starts the story again.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley uses 1 piece of lighting, sound or a prop to create meaning. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses the engagement ring to trace the family’s story. In Act 1 Gerald gives it to Sheila, a sign of the Birling and Croft families joining and of Birling’s business hopes. In Act 2 Sheila hands it back, her first independent decision after hearing Gerald’s story. In Act 3 Gerald offers it again as if the evening can be undone, and she will not take it yet. The telephone then rings. The ring’s return to the start mirrors the play’s circular structure and shows who wants to go back to how things were.
checklist: Chooses a lighting, sound or prop detail
Says when it happens
Explains what it suggests at each point
Links it to structure or character
Explains the effect on the audience
questions.explanation: Staging details are methods. Analyse them like language, saying when they happen and why they matter.

units.title: Structure: entrances, exits and act endings
units.summary: The play has 3 acts in 1 room, each following straight on, and every act ends on a cliffhanger. Entrances and exits are timed for effect.

questions.prompt: How is the play structured?
options: 3 acts in 1 room, each following straight on from the last
questions.explanation: The tension never drops, and the audience lives through the evening in real time with the family.

questions.prompt: Match each act to how it ends.
pairs: The Inspector reappears in the doorway and asks a 1-word question
A telephone call: a girl has died and an inspector is coming
questions.explanation: Each act ends at a moment of high tension, holding the audience across the break.

questions.prompt: Put the confessions in the order they happen in the play.
items: Birling
Sheila
Gerald
Mrs Birling
Eric
questions.explanation: Priestley saves the most personal confessions for last, bringing the guilt closer to the heart of the family.

questions.prompt: Whose confession is about business?
questions.explanation: Birling’s is about business; Sheila’s about spite; Gerald’s about sex and money; Mrs Birling’s about a pregnant girl; Eric’s about the father of the child.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about entrances and exits is true or false.

statements.s: Sheila runs out after seeing the photograph and returns ready to confess.
Gerald stays in the room throughout Act 3.
Eric returns just as his mother has condemned the father.
The Inspector leaves after his final warning.

questions.explanation: Gerald leaves for a walk and misses the final speech. Each exit and entrance is timed for effect.

questions.prompt: Why does Gerald’s exit in Act 2 matter later?
options: He misses the final speech, which helps explain why he believes in a hoax.
He goes to fetch the Chief Constable.
questions.explanation: Being absent for the Inspector’s final words leaves Gerald untouched by them.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Priestley uses structure to make it interesting.’ What did AQA’s 2023 report say about structure?
options: It is not a requirement; comment on it only when it has a clear effect.
It must appear in every paragraph.
It earns marks only on Edexcel.
It should be listed at the start.
questions.explanation: Comment on an opening, an ending, an entrance or the order of confessions when it has a clear effect.
questions.misconception: Treating structure as a box to tick.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of ending each act on a cliffhanger?
options: The audience is held across the break, desperate to know what happens next.
It signals the end of the play.
questions.explanation: The production’s teacher pack calls this technique a cliffhanger. It keeps tension high throughout.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley save the most personal confessions for last?
options: Each step brings the guilt closer to the heart of the family.
The actors needed time to arrive.
questions.explanation: By Act 3 no one in the room can pretend Eva’s death has nothing to do with them.

questions.prompt: AQA’s examiners in 2022 praised answers that explained Priestley’s circular structure. Explain its effect in 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley builds the play in a circle. It opens with the family celebrating and a doorbell announcing an inspector; it ends, after the family think they have escaped, with a telephone call announcing that another inspector is on his way. The return to the start denies the older Birlings and Gerald the relief they thought they had won, and suggests that the lesson will keep coming back until it is learned. For the audience, the circle turns the ending into a question about whether they, too, will change.
checklist: Explains how the ending returns to the beginning
Compares the doorbell and the telephone
Explains the effect on the characters
Explains the effect on the audience
Links structure to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Circular structure is a strong point when you explain what the return to the start achieves.

units.title: Dramatic irony
units.summary: Dramatic irony happens when the audience knows something a character does not. Priestley uses irony from history and irony from the plot.

questions.prompt: Which situation is an example of dramatic irony?
options: A character says a ship cannot sink, and the audience knows it sank.
A pair of characters argue loudly.
questions.explanation: The audience’s knowledge creates the gap. Birling’s Titanic claim is the classic example.

questions.prompt: Match each moment to what the audience knows that the character does not.
pairs: It sank on its first voyage in April 1912
Birling dismisses the chance of war
Mrs Birling demands the father be punished
Eric has been up to a great deal
questions.explanation: The first 2 depend on history; the last 2 on the plot.

questions.prompt: Who jokes “Unless Eric’s been up to something” (Act 1) as the Inspector is announced?
