questions.explanation: Gerald’s joke comes just after Birling has talked about avoiding scandal. By Act 3 it has come true.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Some of the irony depends on history the 1945 audience knew.
Some depends on the audience working things out before the characters.
Dramatic irony means a character is being sarcastic.

questions.explanation: Sarcasm is a character’s tone. Dramatic irony is a gap between the audience’s knowledge and a character’s.

questions.prompt: Priestley had fought in the war that Birling says will not come. How does this sharpen the irony?
options: The playwright and his audience had lived through what Birling dismisses.
It shows Priestley agreed with Birling.
questions.explanation: His audience had lived through 2 world wars, so Birling’s certainty looks dangerously wrong.

questions.prompt: How does dramatic irony build tension in Act 2?
options: The audience waits for Mrs Birling to understand what she is saying.
The audience knows the Inspector’s real name.
questions.explanation: The more certain she sounds, the more the audience dreads the moment she realises.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Priestley uses dramatic irony here.’ What is missing?
options: What the audience knows, what the character does not, and what the gap achieves
Nothing: naming the technique is enough
questions.explanation: Do not stop at naming dramatic irony. Explain the gap and its effect.
questions.misconception: Naming dramatic irony without explaining it.

questions.prompt: Where does the final irony of the play fall?
options: On Birling, who mocks his children moments before the call proves them right
On Sheila, who believes the hoax
On the Inspector, who is arrested
questions.explanation: Birling’s sarcasm about the younger generation comes just before the telephone rings.

questions.prompt: Irony lets the audience feel they know more than the family. How does the ending change this?
options: The final call takes that comfort away: the audience no longer knows what will happen.
questions.explanation: Priestley draws the audience in, then unsettles them, so they too must think about the lesson.

questions.prompt: Explain how Priestley uses dramatic irony to shape the audience’s view of Birling. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses irony from history to teach the audience not to trust Birling. He calls the Titanic “unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable” (Birling, Act 1), and the repetition makes him sound certain just as the audience knows the ship sank that April. He dismisses the chance of war, which came in 1914. Because he is so wrong about the future, the audience is ready to reject his views on workers and community too. The irony returns at the end, when he mocks his children moments before the telephone proves them right.
checklist: Explains what the audience knows that Birling does not
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains the effect on how Birling is judged
Links the irony to his wider views
Notes the final irony at the end
questions.explanation: Strong answers explain the gap in knowledge and what Priestley achieves with it.

units.title: How characters speak
units.summary: Each character’s way of speaking is a clue to who they are and what Priestley wants the audience to think. Explain what the language shows, not just what it is called.

questions.prompt: Match each speaker to their typical sentence form.
pairs: Long, rambling statements full of confident predictions
questions.explanation: Sentence form suggests character: self-importance, control, superiority and new independence.

questions.prompt: How would you describe Eric’s way of speaking?
questions.explanation: His slang refuses to soften what happened. That sets him apart from both parents.

questions.prompt: Birling tells the young men he does not want to lecture them again, then does exactly that. What does this show?
options: He loves his own voice and is used to being listened to.
questions.explanation: His speeches are full of confident claims and business words such as costs and prices.

questions.prompt: How does Gerald speak, especially in Act 3?
options: Smoothly and politely, keen to move on
questions.explanation: His calm reassurance when he offers the ring again shows how easily he wants to forget.

questions.prompt: The central lines of the final speech are 3 short statements, each beginning with ‘We’. What does the pronoun do?
options: It includes the audience, making the idea sound like a simple shared truth.
It shows the Inspector is talking about himself.
It refers only to the police.
It makes the speech sound uncertain.
questions.explanation: Plain words and the inclusive pronoun turn the message outwards.

questions.prompt: A student writes ‘Priestley uses the adjective unsinkable’ and stops there. What did AQA’s 2023 report say about this?
options: Labelling word classes leads to stifled, formulaic discussion.
questions.explanation: Explain what the language shows about the character and what Priestley wants the audience to think.
questions.misconception: Labelling word classes without explaining effect.

questions.prompt: Who uses the childish word “Mummy” (Act 1)?
questions.explanation: Sheila starts with childish words and moves to sarcasm and challenge by Act 3.

questions.prompt: Mrs Birling refers to Eva by her class rather than her name. What does the phrasing do?
options: It treats a person as a category.
It shows she knew Eva well.
questions.explanation: Her formal, superior language matches the way she judges. Nothing a girl of that class says can be believed.

questions.prompt: Why does the Inspector sometimes use shocking physical detail?
options: To cut through polite language and force the family to face the reality of the death
questions.explanation: He speaks plainly most of the time and uses brutal images when he needs them.

questions.prompt: Compare how 2 characters speak and explain what Priestley shows through the difference. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley contrasts Birling’s long speeches with the Inspector’s short, plain sentences. Birling talks at length, full of confident predictions and business words, because he is used to being listened to; he even says he does not want to lecture the young men before doing so. The Inspector asks direct questions and states plain truths, and in his final speech he builds to the line “We are responsible for each other” (Inspector, Act 3). The difference in language becomes a difference in values: Birling’s words serve himself, while the Inspector’s are meant for everyone.
checklist: Compares 2 speakers clearly
Describes sentence forms or vocabulary accurately
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains what each style shows
Links the contrast to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Language analysis earns credit when it explains character and purpose, not when it labels words.

units.title: The ending
units.summary: The family relax when the evening seems to be a hoax, then a telephone call announces a death and an inspector on his way. Priestley never explains who Goole was.

questions.prompt: What interrupts the family’s relief at the very end?
questions.explanation: The opening was interrupted by a doorbell; the ending by a telephone. Both announce an inspector.

questions.prompt: Put the final minutes of the play in order.
items: Gerald returns with news that there is no Inspector Goole
The Chief Constable confirms it
A call to the Infirmary finds no dead girl
Gerald offers Sheila the ring again
Birling mocks his children
The telephone rings
questions.explanation: Relief builds step by step, so the final call lands at the moment the older characters feel safest.

questions.prompt: Match each reading of the ending to what it means.
pairs: The family will face the questions again, now knowing the answers
The older Birlings and Gerald are caught when they think they are safe
Time repeats until the lesson is learned
Ignoring the lesson leads to suffering
questions.explanation: Any of these can be argued. Choose 1 and explain how the ending supports it.

questions.prompt: Which character reports the news from the final telephone call?
questions.explanation: Birling, who has just been mocking his children, must tell the family that a girl has died and a police inspector is on his way.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of the opening to its echo at the end.
pairs: Gerald offers the ring and Sheila will not take it yet
Birling lectures the young men with confidence
Birling mocks his children, then falls silent
questions.explanation: The ending mirrors the opening, so the audience sees how much and how little has changed.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The play ends with the family staring at each other.
Priestley explains who Inspector Goole was.
The call to the Infirmary finds no dead girl.

questions.explanation: Priestley leaves the mystery unsolved, which keeps attention on the family’s actions.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The ending proves the Inspector was a ghost.’ What is the problem?
options: Priestley never explains who he was; the ending supports several readings.
The Inspector is definitely a real policeman.
The Inspector returns at the end to prove he is human.
There is no Inspector in the play.
questions.explanation: Present a reading as a reading. What matters is that the family’s actions were real.
questions.misconception: Treating 1 reading of the ending as proven fact.

questions.prompt: How does the ending sort the characters?
options: The call confirms what Sheila and Eric know but shocks the older Birlings and Gerald.
questions.explanation: Those who had decided nothing was their fault are caught out.

questions.prompt: Why is the ending a strong place to finish an essay on almost any theme?
options: It is Priestley’s final word, so a closing paragraph on it can pull the argument together.
It is the shortest part of the play.
Examiners only read the last paragraph.
It has no connection to the themes.
questions.explanation: The telephone call tests responsibility, the generations, time and class at once.

questions.prompt: Explain what the final minutes of the play do to the characters and to the audience. Write 1 paragraph.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley lets the family believe they have escaped, then brings the story back with a single telephone call. Gerald’s news, the Chief Constable and the Infirmary all seem to prove a hoax, so the older Birlings and Gerald relax, and Birling mocks his children. Then he must report that “a police inspector is on his way here” (Birling, Act 3). The ending tests who has really learned: Sheila and Eric already accept their guilt, while the others are caught out. By leaving the Inspector unexplained, Priestley keeps the focus on what the family did and leaves his audience with the warning.
checklist: Explains how relief builds before the call
Uses a short, accurate quotation
Explains how the ending sorts the characters
Comments on the unsolved mystery
Links to Priestley’s purpose for the audience
questions.explanation: The ending is Priestley’s verdict. Strong answers explain what it does to the characters and the audience.

units.title: Reading the question
units.summary: Read the question twice, underline the focus and the command words, and decide your own answer before you plan. Most weak answers go wrong in the first minute.

questions.prompt: Match each command word or phrase to what it asks you to do.
pairs: Investigate in depth, considering more than 1 angle
Weigh the statement and reach a clear judgement
Why something matters to the play and its message
Set 2 things side by side: similarities and differences
questions.explanation: Command words tell you the shape of the answer. Misreading them is an easy way to lose marks.

questions.prompt: What should you do first with an exam question?
options: Read it twice and underline the focus and command words
Write out every quotation you know
Count the marks on the page
questions.explanation: Then decide what you think the answer is before you plan.

questions.prompt: Match each board to how its questions are usually worded.
pairs: How does Priestley present...? with 2 bullet points
A short quotation, then a question with a reminder about context
Compare 2 printed extracts, then explore another moment
A statement and a task, referring to the extract and the whole play
questions.explanation: Knowing the wording in advance means fewer surprises in the exam.

questions.prompt: What does a question beginning ‘How does Priestley present...’ ask you to do?
options: Argue about his methods and their effects
Give your opinion of the play
questions.explanation: Present means you must discuss methods: dramatic irony, the ending, stage directions, language.

questions.prompt: An Edexcel question opens with a quotation from Sheila. What did Pearson’s 2024 report warn against?
questions.explanation: Treat the quotation as a way in to the whole play, not the limit of your answer.
questions.misconception: Writing only about the speaker of the Edexcel quotation.

questions.prompt: The question asks how Priestley presents the idea that some characters refuse to change. Which characters are the main focus?
options: Mr and Mrs Birling and Gerald, with Sheila and Eric as a contrast
questions.explanation: The focus points to the characters who refuse. Using the ones who change as a contrast sharpens the argument.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: A theme question is best answered as a list of characters.
You should decide your own answer before you plan.
‘At different points’ means you should range across the play.

questions.explanation: If the question names a theme, organise your answer by ideas about that theme.

questions.prompt: Which opening is organised by ideas rather than characters, for a question on class?
options: Priestley shows class as a system: the factory, the shop and the charity all work for the wealthy.
First I will write about Birling, then Sheila, then Gerald.
Class is a theme in the play.
Birling is rich and Eva is poor.
questions.explanation: An idea-led opening gives every paragraph a job. A list of characters tends to become a list of crimes.

questions.prompt: Which is the best 1-sentence argument for ‘How does Priestley present attitudes to money?’
options: Priestley shows money protecting the older Birlings from responsibility, while the young begin to see past it.
There is a lot of money in the play.
Birling has money and Eva does not have money.
Money is the root of all evil.
questions.explanation: A good argument answers the question, takes a view and hints at the route through the play.

questions.prompt: Unpick this question and write your argument in 1 or 2 sentences: How does Priestley present the idea of guilt?
questions.model: Model answer: Focus: guilt, both who feels it and who refuses it; the command ‘present’ means I must discuss methods. Argument: Priestley shows guilt as something the young accept and the old refuse, and uses the Inspector’s summing-up and the final telephone call to insist that guilt is shared, whether or not a crime was committed.
checklist: Identifies the focus (guilt)
Notes what ‘present’ asks for
States a clear argument that answers the question
Hints at moments or methods to use
Treats the characters as Priestley’s constructs
questions.explanation: Time spent unpicking the question saves a paragraph that answers a different one.

units.title: Writing about Priestley’s purpose
units.summary: The characters are not real people: Priestley invented them to make his audience think. Keep the writer in view by writing about what he does and why.

questions.prompt: What do examiners reward when you write about characters?
options: Keeping Priestley in view: what he does with a character and why
Saying which character you like best
Guessing what happens after the play
questions.explanation: AQA’s 2020 report praised writing about Birling as a device used by Priestley for dramatic effect.

questions.prompt: Match each verb to its meaning when you write about Priestley.
pairs: Sets 2 characters or ideas against each other
questions.explanation: Verbs like these keep the playwright as the subject of your sentences.

questions.prompt: Which of these were Priestley’s aims, according to the guide?
options: Persuade a 1945 audience that people are responsible for each other
Attack selfish capitalism and class prejudice
Celebrate Edwardian society as it was
Show hope in the young, who can learn and change
questions.explanation: He also warned that ignoring the lesson leads to suffering, as 2 wars had shown. He did not celebrate 1912.

questions.prompt: Which sentence treats the Inspector as a construct?
options: Priestley uses the Inspector’s control of the questioning to drive the plot and voice his own beliefs.
The Inspector works everything out by himself.
I think the Inspector is the best character.
questions.explanation: The first sentence names Priestley and explains a purpose. The others describe the Inspector as if he were real.
questions.misconception: Writing about characters as if they were real people.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘This makes the reader feel sad.’ What did AQA’s 2023 report say about this kind of comment?
options: It often produced general, unsupported comments.
It earns full marks for personal response.
It is required in every paragraph.
It is only a problem on Edexcel.
questions.explanation: Give your own answer to the question, with reasons from the play, and write about the audience rather than the reader.
questions.misconception: Using ‘this makes the reader feel’ as personal response.

questions.prompt: How could you improve the sentence ‘Edna has a boring job’?
options: Priestley keeps Edna, a maid, on stage so that a working-class woman is present while the family discuss another they ignored.
Edna has a really boring job as a maid.
Edna should get a better job.
Edna is the maid and does the dishes.
questions.explanation: The rewrite names Priestley and explains why the detail matters.

questions.prompt: When is it worth offering an alternative reading?
options: When it deepens your argument, as with Mrs Birling’s possible self-protection
In every paragraph, to be safe
questions.explanation: Forcing ‘it could mean this, but it could also mean the opposite’ weakens an answer. Use alternatives with purpose.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each sentence treats the character as Priestley’s construct.

statements.s: Priestley makes Birling pompous and wrong so that his audience will reject his views.
Sheila feels really bad about what she did.
By keeping Eva offstage, Priestley makes the audience notice how little power she had.

questions.explanation: Constructed sentences name Priestley and explain a choice. The false one describes Sheila’s feelings as if she were real.

questions.prompt: Choose the best verb: ‘Priestley ___ the audience to judge Birling by showing him wrong about the Titanic.’
questions.explanation: ‘Invites’ captures how Priestley leads the audience to a view without stating it.

questions.prompt: Write 1 paragraph about Eric that treats him as Priestley’s construct throughout.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses Eric to show that the older generation’s values have failed their own children. He gives Eric the most disturbing confession, so the audience cannot simply admire him, yet he also makes Eric the only man in the family who openly accepts his guilt. When Eric tells his father he could never have gone to him for help, Priestley exposes how empty Birling’s talk of looking after his family really is. Through Eric’s anger, Priestley invites his 1945 audience to side with a generation willing to learn.
checklist: Names Priestley as the subject of most sentences
Explains choices Priestley makes with Eric
Uses precise verbs such as exposes or invites
Links Eric to Priestley’s purpose
Avoids describing Eric as if he were real
questions.explanation: Every sentence should say what Priestley does and why.

units.title: Planning in 5 minutes
units.summary: A 5-minute plan gives you an argument, 4 or 5 moments from across the play, a method for each and context where it helps. Order the paragraphs so the argument builds.

questions.prompt: Put the 5 planning steps in order.
items: Decide your argument in 1 sentence
Choose 4 or 5 moments from across the play
Note 1 method for each moment
Add context only where it explains purpose
Order the paragraphs so the argument builds
questions.explanation: The argument comes first because it decides which moments matter.

questions.prompt: How many moments should a 5-minute plan include?
options: 4 or 5, from across the play, including the beginning and the end
questions.explanation: Covering the whole play, including the ending, shows range.

questions.prompt: For Eduqas, how much context should your plan include?
options: None, unless it explains Priestley’s purpose in a method
questions.explanation: Eduqas does not reward AO3 on this question.

questions.prompt: Why end a plan with the play’s final minutes?
options: The ending is Priestley’s final word and pulls the argument together.
The ending has the most quotations.
questions.explanation: Ordering the paragraphs so the argument builds to the telephone call gives a strong finish.

questions.prompt: AQA’s examiners linked short, shapeless answers to one thing. What?
questions.explanation: They also noted that a short thesis-style introduction helps at every level.
questions.misconception: Skipping the plan to save time.

questions.prompt: You are planning: How does Priestley present Gerald as a character who is hard to judge? Which moments fit?
options: The stage direction on his entrance
His absence from the final speech
questions.explanation: Stealing the money is Eric’s act. Mixing up the 2 young men is a mistake examiners report.

questions.prompt: Which is a usable argument for a plan?
options: Priestley makes Gerald sympathetic so that his return to the older Birlings’ side is more troubling.
questions.explanation: A plan’s argument must answer the question and take a view.

questions.prompt: A plan on Sheila ends with a bullet called ‘Limits: guilt partly about herself; future left open’. What does it add?
options: A weighed counter-point that makes the argument more convincing
questions.explanation: Showing the limits of Sheila’s change keeps the argument believable.

questions.prompt: You are planning an answer on Birling. Match each moment to a method you could analyse.
questions.explanation: 1 method for each moment keeps every paragraph analytical.

questions.prompt: Write a 5-minute plan for: How does Priestley present Mrs Birling as a powerful woman?
questions.model: Model plan: Argument: Priestley gives Mrs Birling real power within the limits open to women of her class, and shows her using it against a weaker woman. Moments: her status as her husband’s social superior (stage direction, Act 1); her control of the charity committee; her orders to the Inspector; her demand that the father be punished, which turns on Eric; her denial at the end. Methods: stage directions, commands, dramatic irony, the ending. Context (if your board rewards it): no welfare state in 1912, so charity was power; women had no vote.
checklist: States a clear argument
Chooses 4 or 5 moments from across the play
Notes a method for each
Adds context only where it helps
Ends with the play’s final minutes
questions.explanation: A good plan is short, but it already contains the whole argument.

units.title: Writing a strong paragraph
units.summary: A strong paragraph starts from an idea about the question and uses the play to prove it. Short quotations and context belong inside the point, not after it.

questions.prompt: How should a strong paragraph begin?
options: With an idea that answers the question
With the date of the play
With a retelling of the plot
questions.explanation: There is no magic formula. Start from an idea and use the play to prove it.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Short, embedded quotations are better than long ones.
Every paragraph must follow a fixed point-evidence-explain formula.
Context should be part of the point, not a fact added at the end.

questions.explanation: AQA’s examiners have warned that rigid frameworks can hold students back.

questions.prompt: Match each sentence opener to the way it weaves in context.
pairs: In 1912 a woman like Eva had no vote, so...
questions.explanation: Each opener ties context to a point about the play.

questions.prompt: Match each sentence opener to the method it introduces.
pairs: By placing Eric’s entrance at the end of Act 2...
The harsher lighting that comes with the Inspector...
The audience knows what Birling does not...
questions.explanation: Name the method only when it adds something to your point.

questions.prompt: What did AQA’s examiners warn about rigid point-evidence-explain frameworks?
options: They can lead students to break a quotation down word by word instead of linking it to ideas.
They are required by every board.
They should be used for every sentence.
questions.explanation: A paragraph should serve an idea, not a formula.
questions.misconception: Believing a fixed formula guarantees a strong paragraph.

questions.prompt: Put the parts of a strong paragraph in a sensible order.
items: An idea that answers the question
A short embedded quotation, analysed
A second reference that develops the idea
Context that explains the effect on the audience
A link to a method or the wider play
questions.explanation: This is the shape of the model paragraph on Mrs Birling in the guide. The order can vary, but every part serves the idea.

questions.prompt: Which sentence embeds a quotation best?
options: Birling dismisses “community and all that nonsense” (Birling, Act 1) as if the idea were a joke, which Priestley will make him regret.
Birling says a quotation. It shows he is selfish.
Here is a quotation from Act 1 that shows Birling’s views.
Birling is selfish, as shown by a long speech.
questions.explanation: The quotation sits inside the writer’s own sentence and is followed straight away by its effect.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a retelling rather than an idea?
options: Then Mrs Birling is questioned and says she refused the girl.
Priestley presents Mrs Birling as blinded by her own superiority.
Priestley uses Mrs Birling to show charity as a kind of power.
Mrs Birling’s certainty becomes the trap that condemns her son.
questions.explanation: Retelling says what happens. An idea says what Priestley is doing.

questions.prompt: A paragraph ends: ‘In 1912 there was no welfare state.’ What is the problem?
options: The context is bolted on rather than linked to the point.
It is too short to be a sentence.
questions.explanation: The fact is true, but it needs to explain why the moment matters.

questions.prompt: Write 1 paragraph answering: How does Priestley present Gerald’s attitude to women? Use a short quotation and a method.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley presents Gerald as a man whose kindness to women is mixed with a sense of ownership. He rescues Daisy from Meggarty and gives her rooms, yet he makes her his mistress and ends it when it suits him. His contempt for the other women at the Palace bar, “hard-eyed dough-faced women” (Gerald, Act 2), shows that he judges women by their looks and class. Sheila’s sarcasm exposes the gap between his self-image and his actions, and Priestley lets a 1945 audience, aware of how much women’s lives had changed, see that gap clearly.
checklist: Opens with an idea that answers the question
Uses a short, embedded quotation
Names or shows a method
Weaves in context if your board rewards it
Ends by linking to the wider play or purpose
questions.explanation: Every sentence should move the argument forward.

units.title: OCR: comparing with an unseen extract
units.summary: OCR’s question has 2 parts worth 20 marks each: (a) compares a printed play extract with an unseen modern drama extract; (b) explores another moment in the play.

questions.prompt: How many marks is each part of OCR’s question worth?
questions.explanation: Part (a) and part (b) are worth 20 marks each.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: In part (a) you compare an extract from the play with an unseen modern drama extract.
In part (b) you write about the same extract again.
AO4 is not marked on this section.

questions.explanation: Part (b) asks for another moment in An Inspector Calls linked to the same idea.

questions.prompt: What should you write about in part (a)?
options: The whole of An Inspector Calls
questions.explanation: The paper tells you to focus only on the extracts. Save the rest of the play for part (b).

questions.prompt: Match each connective to what it signals.
pairs: A difference, starting a new point
questions.explanation: Comparison connectives keep your answer comparative from start to finish.

questions.prompt: A student writes 3 paragraphs on Extract 1, then 3 on Extract 2. What is the better approach?
options: Compare throughout, moving between the extracts in each paragraph.
questions.explanation: OCR rewards close comparison. Separate halves make the comparison the examiner’s job, not yours.
questions.misconception: Writing about 1 extract and then the other.

questions.prompt: What makes a strong part (b) answer?
options: A tour of the whole play
A comparison with the unseen extract
questions.explanation: 1 moment explored closely is better than a quick tour.

questions.prompt: What timing did the June 2024 paper advise?
options: About 45 minutes for (a) and 30 minutes for (b)
Equal time for both parts, 60 minutes each
questions.explanation: The longer time for (a) reflects the work of comparing 2 extracts closely.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you compare in part (a)?
options: The situation and the characters’ experiences
questions.explanation: The effect on an audience also belongs in the list. Biography of the writers does not.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is genuinely comparative?
options: Both extracts show a parent refusing responsibility for workers, but where Birling argues at length, the other parent falls silent.
The second extract is set in a bakery.
I liked the first extract more.
questions.explanation: A comparative sentence holds both extracts together and points to a similarity and a difference.

questions.prompt: For part (b) on family tension, choose 1 moment from An Inspector Calls and explain why it is a good choice. Then write your opening 2 sentences.
questions.model: Model answer: Choice: the end of Act 2, when Mrs Birling demands that the father be punished and Eric walks in, because tension within the family peaks there and Priestley uses several methods at once. Opening: Priestley builds family tension at the end of Act 2 through dramatic irony, as Mrs Birling insists the young father be made an example of while the audience realises he is her son. Sheila’s pleading and Eric’s silent, distressed entrance turn a public interrogation into a private family crisis.
checklist: Chooses a moment different from the printed extract
Explains why the moment suits the idea
Opens with an idea about Priestley’s methods
Stays focused on 1 moment
Uses accurate detail from the moment
questions.explanation: Part (b) rewards depth: 1 moment, analysed closely.

units.title: Eduqas: working from the extract
units.summary: Eduqas prints an extract and asks about the whole play, for 40 marks including 5 for AO4. Context is not assessed, so put your time into analysis.

questions.prompt: How many of Eduqas’s 40 marks are for spelling, punctuation, vocabulary and sentence structure?
questions.explanation: Eduqas gives 5 marks to AO4 on this question.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: You should refer to the extract and the play as a whole.
Context (AO3) is assessed in this section.
The paper advises about 45 minutes.

questions.explanation: Eduqas’s 2025 report advised including context only when closely tied to the play, for example to explain Priestley’s intentions.

questions.prompt: Put this 45-minute route in order.
items: Read the question and the extract
Plan your argument and 3 other moments
Write about the extract closely
Write about the other moments
Check spelling of names and key words
questions.explanation: The guide suggests about 5, 5, 10, 20 and 5 minutes for these steps.

questions.prompt: According to Eduqas’s 2025 report, which route through an extract question is valid?
options: Any sensible route: extract first, the text in order, or moving between them
questions.explanation: The report said all approaches are valid, and most students now avoid spending too long on the extract.

questions.prompt: A student plans 2 paragraphs of historical background for an Eduqas answer. What is the advice?
options: Cut them: time spent on history is time taken from analysis.
questions.explanation: Context earns nothing extra here. Close analysis of the extract and other moments does.
questions.misconception: Spending Eduqas time on context.

questions.prompt: In 2023 Eduqas asked about reactions to the discovery of truths, with an extract from the end of Act 2. Where might a strong answer start?
options: Mrs Birling’s confident demands collapsing as she realises the father is Eric
questions.explanation: Start with the extract, then move to Sheila at Milwards, Act 3 and the telephone call.

questions.prompt: Which spelling slip in Gerald’s stage direction did Eduqas’s 2025 report note?
questions.explanation: Learn the spelling well-bred, along with Priestley, Birling and Sheila.
questions.misconception: Spelling well-bred as well-bread.

questions.prompt: Which of these earn marks on Eduqas?
options: Close analysis of language, structure and staging in the extract
Well-chosen moments from the rest of the play
Lists of quotations written out before you begin
questions.explanation: Accurate spelling and varied sentences also earn up to 5 marks. History and quotation lists earn nothing extra.

questions.prompt: Eduqas’s 2025 report found 2 details used well in answers about Gerald. Why do such details help?
options: Small, precise details show you know the whole play.
They are the only details examiners accept.
They avoid the need for an argument.
They replace analysis of the extract.
questions.explanation: The ring and Gerald’s absence from the final speech were both praised.

questions.prompt: Plan an Eduqas answer on: How does Priestley present the Inspector’s power? Start from an extract of the final speech and list 3 other moments.
questions.model: Model plan: Argument: Priestley gives the Inspector a moral power that outlasts his presence. Extract: the summing-up and final speech, with short statements, the move from 1 girl to millions and a closing warning. Other moments: his entrance, when the lighting turns harsh and he interrupts Birling; his control of the photograph, shown 1 person at a time; his refusal to be impressed by Birling’s rank. Ending: the family argue after he leaves, and the telephone call shows his power has not ended. No context paragraph.
checklist: States a clear argument
Identifies methods in the extract
Chooses 3 well-spread moments from the rest of the play
Leaves out context paragraphs
Ends with the play’s final minutes
questions.explanation: On Eduqas, every minute should go into analysis of the play.

units.title: Model answer (1)
units.summary: The model essay argues that Birling’s refusal to learn is Priestley’s warning to 1945. Each paragraph moves that argument forward.

questions.prompt: What is the argument of the model essay on Birling?
options: Birling’s refusal to learn is Priestley’s warning to his 1945 audience.
Birling changes completely by the end.
Birling is the hero of the play.
questions.explanation: The argument appears in the first sentence and runs through every paragraph.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the model essay is true or false.

statements.s: It treats Birling as a construct with a purpose.
It retells the plot act by act without an argument.
It uses short, embedded quotations.

questions.explanation: The annotations show each part doing a job: argument, method, context.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of the model essay to the assessment objective it targets.
pairs: A clear, conceptual argument in the first sentence
A method named and its effect explained
Context tied to the effect of a quotation
questions.explanation: AQA marks AO1 and AO2 at 12 each, AO3 at 6 and AO4 at 4.

questions.prompt: The model essay analyses Birling calling low wages his duty. What does it argue the word does?
options: Turns self-interest into a moral principle, so he never has to feel guilty
Shows he agrees with the Inspector
questions.explanation: Close analysis of 1 word, linked to character and theme, is AO2 at its best.

questions.prompt: The essay notes that the doorbell rings during Birling’s speech. What kind of point is this?
options: Structural: the timing of an entrance
questions.explanation: The timing makes it seem as though the play itself is answering him.

questions.prompt: What separates a Level 6 answer from a Level 4 answer in its use of quotations?
options: Level 6 uses short, precise references woven into sentences; Level 4 uses relevant ones, sometimes long.
questions.explanation: Precision and integration matter more than length.
questions.misconception: Believing longer quotations reach higher levels.

questions.prompt: Put the route of the model essay in order.
items: Act 1 speeches and dramatic irony
The interrogation: duty and status
Act 3: relief and mocking the young
The final telephone call
questions.explanation: The route covers the whole play and builds to the ending.

questions.prompt: Why does the model compare Birling with Eric in Act 3?
options: The contrast sharpens the argument about refusing to learn.
Because the question asks about Eric.
questions.explanation: Eric’s acceptance of guilt makes Birling’s refusal stand out.

questions.prompt: The model says Birling’s ‘failure to learn is what the character is for’. What skill does this show?
options: Treating a character as Priestley’s construct
Giving a personal opinion of Birling
questions.explanation: Asking what a character is for keeps Priestley at the centre.
questions.misconception: Writing about characters as if they were real people.

questions.prompt: Write your own paragraph (not copied from the model) on how Priestley uses Birling’s status to show he refuses to learn.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley shows that Birling’s status makes him unable to learn, because he expects it to protect him. He reminds the Inspector of his past as an alderman and his place on the bench, and hopes for a knighthood, as though rank could excuse what he did. The Inspector’s reply, that public men have duties as well as advantages, rejects this idea. Even in Act 3, Birling’s first worry is the scandal, not the girl. Priestley shows a 1945 audience that men who think status puts them above judgement will never change.
checklist: Opens with an argument linked to the question
Uses accurate references to Birling’s status
Includes the Inspector’s counter-view
Moves to Act 3 to show no change
Links to the 1945 audience
questions.explanation: Use the model as a pattern, not a script: your paragraph should build its own argument.

units.title: Model answer (2)
units.summary: The model ends with the telephone call as Priestley’s verdict and a conclusion that returns to the argument. It reaches the top level by arguing about the whole play.

questions.prompt: How does the model deliver Priestley’s final judgement on Birling?
options: Through structure: the telephone call at the end
Through a list of Birling’s mistakes
questions.explanation: The circular ending denies Birling the escape he thought he had won.

questions.prompt: Match each AQA level to its mark range.
questions.explanation: Levels are paraphrased from the AQA 8702/2 mark scheme (June 2023).

questions.prompt: What should a conclusion do?
options: Apologise for running out of time
questions.explanation: The model’s conclusion turns Birling into a warning, rather than retelling what happens.

questions.prompt: Match each Level 4 feature to the Level 6 feature that improves on it.
pairs: Explains what Birling says and why it is wrong
Argues about what Priestley is doing with Birling and why
Uses short, precise references woven into sentences
Names methods such as dramatic irony
Explores how methods shape the audience’s response
Makes context part of the argument about purpose
questions.explanation: Each step up is about doing more with the same material.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about Level 6 is true or false.

statements.s: It is critical and exploratory.
It uses precise references chosen with judgement.
It is mostly a retelling of the plot.

questions.explanation: A Level 6 answer argues about the whole task and explores context through detailed links.

questions.prompt: A conclusion reads: ‘In Act 1 Birling talks, in Act 2 his wife is questioned and in Act 3 the phone rings.’ What is wrong?
options: It summarises the plot instead of returning to the argument.
It uses the wrong act numbers.
questions.explanation: A conclusion should state what the essay has shown about Priestley’s purpose.
questions.misconception: Ending an essay with a plot summary.

questions.prompt: What makes context reach the top level?
options: It is part of the argument about Priestley’s purpose.
It comes in a separate paragraph.
It includes as many dates as possible.
questions.explanation: Context explored through detailed links to the text is a Level 6 feature.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is stronger?
options: By making Birling comic and wrong, then catching him out in the final seconds, Priestley turns him into a warning about a society that will not learn.
Birling is a bad man and I did not like him.
That is everything that happens to Birling in the play.
questions.explanation: The first returns to the argument and names Priestley’s methods.

questions.prompt: The model links the Inspector’s warning to an audience who had lived through 2 world wars. Which objective does this target most?
questions.explanation: Context tied to the effect of a line on the audience is AO3.

questions.prompt: Write a conclusion for an essay on: How does Priestley use Sheila to show that people can change?
questions.model: Model conclusion: Priestley uses Sheila to prove that change is possible, but he never makes it easy. She moves from a sheltered daughter delighted with her ring to the one member of the family who will not let the others pretend, yet her guilt is partly about herself and her future is left open by the final telephone call. That openness is the point: Priestley hands the work of change to his 1945 audience, asking them to learn as Sheila did, before the lesson has to be taught again.
checklist: Returns to the argument
Sums up how Sheila changes without retelling the plot
Acknowledges the limits of her change
Refers to the ending
Links to Priestley’s purpose for the audience
questions.explanation: A conclusion should leave the examiner with your argument, not a list of events.

units.title: Edexcel: putting context at the centre
units.summary: Edexcel gives 16 marks to your response, 16 to context and 8 to accurate writing, with none for AO2. Keep context running through the essay in short, specific points.

questions.prompt: How are Edexcel’s 40 marks split?
questions.explanation: There are no marks for AO2 on this question.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Context should sit in a separate paragraph at the end.
Each question opens with a short quotation from the play.
Pearson’s 2019 report suggested about 50 minutes.

questions.explanation: Context must run through the essay in short, specific points.

questions.prompt: Where should context appear in an Edexcel essay?
options: Throughout, in short, specific points tied to moments
questions.explanation: The model frames its argument with context from the first sentence.

questions.prompt: Match each Edexcel level to its description (AO1 and AO3).
pairs: Developed response; sustained comment on context
Relevant, sound response; sound comment on context
Largely narrative, with some awareness of context
questions.explanation: Paraphrased from the Pearson Edexcel 1ET0/01 mark scheme (2024). AO4 is marked separately out of 8.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2019 report noted that even an excellent answer had one weakness with context. What was it?
options: It became a little lengthy at times.
It was about the wrong country.
It was in the wrong language.
questions.explanation: Keep each contextual point to a sentence or 2, tied to a moment in the play.
questions.misconception: Letting context dominate an Edexcel essay.

questions.prompt: The model’s stimulus quotation is “community and all that nonsense” (Birling, Act 1). How should it be used?
options: As a way in to an argument about the whole play
As the only evidence in the essay
questions.explanation: The quotation launches the argument about wealth and status, which then ranges across the play.

questions.prompt: Which context best explains the effect of Mrs Birling’s refusal on an Edexcel essay about wealth and status?
options: In 1912 there was no welfare state, and the 1945 audience would soon see the Beveridge plan become the welfare state.
questions.explanation: The context explains why the refusal would shock Priestley’s audience.

questions.prompt: Edexcel gives no marks for AO2. Why do you still need to explain how the play works?
options: It builds your argument and response to the text (AO1).
You do not: ignore methods entirely.
questions.explanation: Methods support your argument even when they are not marked separately.

questions.prompt: Which of these fit the plan for the rest of the model essay?
options: Mrs Birling’s charity, with help as a favour before the welfare state
The Crofts and the marriage as a business merger
Sheila and Eric rejecting their parents’ values
A paragraph listing every date from 1894 to 1984
questions.explanation: The plan ends with the telephone call. A list of dates would be bolted-on context.

questions.prompt: Write an Edexcel-style paragraph on attitudes to wealth and status, weaving in context.
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses Sheila and Eric to show the next generation rejecting their parents’ attitude to wealth. Eric asks why workers should not try for higher wages when owners try for the highest prices, and Sheila insists that girls like Eva are people, not cheap labour. In 1912 their father’s view was common among employers, but Priestley was writing for a 1945 audience who had just voted Labour in a landslide, hoping the young would build a fairer country. The children’s challenge therefore stands for the change the audience had chosen.
checklist: Makes an argument about wealth and status
Uses references to Sheila and Eric
Includes 1912 context
Includes 1945 context tied to the effect on the audience
Keeps context short and woven in
questions.explanation: On Edexcel, context should sharpen every point rather than sit apart.

units.title: Mistakes examiners keep seeing
units.summary: Recent examiners’ reports name the same errors: retelling the plot, bolted-on context, wrong speakers and muddled dates. Each has a simple fix.

questions.prompt: Which mistake did AQA’s 2020 report name?
options: Retelling the plot instead of arguing about Priestley’s choices
questions.explanation: Treat characters as constructs with a purpose.

questions.prompt: Match each mistake to its fix.
pairs: Listing each character’s crime on a theme question
Organise by ideas and use characters as evidence
Show the idea through a moment, such as the strike
Writing out lists of quotations before starting
Leaving Gerald out of an answer on Eva
questions.explanation: Each fix comes from the same report that named the mistake.

questions.prompt: What should you call the play’s first audience?
questions.explanation: Pearson’s 2025 report noted students calling the audience Victorian or Jacobean.
questions.misconception: Calling the audience Victorian or Jacobean.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Pearson’s 2025 report warned against applying critical theory such as Freud loosely.
Examiners reported lines given to the wrong character, especially Eric and Gerald.
Forced terms such as ‘semantic field’ always earn extra marks.

questions.explanation: Discuss characterisation, setting, structure and symbols instead of forcing terms.

questions.prompt: You are unsure of the exact words of a quotation. What is the safest choice?
options: Refer clearly to the moment instead
Give it to a different character
questions.explanation: Invented quotations were reported by Pearson and Eduqas in 2025. A reference to the moment counts as evidence.
questions.misconception: Inventing quotations under pressure.

questions.prompt: Eduqas’s 2025 report noted students writing out lists of quotations before starting. Why is this a problem?
options: It uses time without earning marks.
It makes the answer too short.
questions.explanation: Plan briefly, then write. Quotations earn credit only inside an argument.

questions.prompt: Pearson’s 2025 report warned about critical theory such as Freud. What should you do instead?
options: Keep to your own argument about the play.
questions.explanation: Theory applied loosely distracts from what Priestley does.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2022 report told students not to fret about slightly misquoting. Why?
options: A nearly word-perfect reference used intelligently is worth more than a perfect quotation with nothing to say.
Quotations do not matter at all.
Examiners do not know the play.
questions.explanation: Use short quotations you are sure of, and spend your effort on what they show.

questions.prompt: Spot the error: ‘Gerald admits he stole money from his father’s office to give to Eva.’
options: It was Eric who stole the money; Gerald kept Daisy as his mistress.
questions.explanation: Pearson’s and Eduqas’s examiners both reported answers that confused the 2 young men.

questions.prompt: Rewrite this weak paragraph to fix its mistakes: ‘Priestley’s Victorian audience would hate Birling. First Birling sacks Eva. Then Sheila gets her sacked. Then Gerald. Birling is a bourgeois capitalist pig.’
questions.model: Model paragraph: Priestley uses Birling to show his 1945 audience the attitudes they were being asked to leave behind. When his workers strike for higher wages, Birling sacks the leaders and calls keeping costs down his duty, so self-interest is dressed up as a principle. That first dismissal sets off the chain that leads, through Sheila’s complaint and Gerald’s affair, to Eva’s death. An audience that had just voted for a welfare state would see how much power men like Birling held over workers like her.
checklist: Corrects the audience to 1945
Replaces the list of events with an idea
Replaces the slogan with evidence from the play
Uses accurate detail about the strike
Links to Priestley’s purpose
questions.explanation: Every fix here matches a mistake named in a recent examiners’ report.

units.title: Spelling, punctuation and AO4
units.summary: AO4 is worth 4 marks on AQA, 8 on Edexcel, 5 on Eduqas and none on OCR. Spell the names right every time and embed quotations correctly.

questions.prompt: Which spelling is correct?
questions.explanation: The name has an e before the y: Priestley.

questions.prompt: Spot the words that are spelled correctly.
questions.explanation: The correct spellings are Birling and responsibility.

questions.prompt: Match each board to its AO4 marks on this question.
questions.explanation: Know your board’s figure so you can judge how much checking time to save.

questions.prompt: How should you show the title of the play in a handwritten exam?
questions.explanation: In print it appears in italics; in handwriting, underline it.

questions.prompt: Which spelling of Gerald’s stage direction word is correct?
questions.explanation: Eduqas’s 2025 report noted ‘bread’ for ‘bred’. Bred means brought up.
questions.misconception: Spelling well-bred as well-bread.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each rule about quotations is true or false.

statements.s: Use an ellipsis only to show that words have been left out.
Use single quotation marks for a quotation inside a quotation.
Long quotations should always be copied out in full.

questions.explanation: Embed short quotations and keep the meaning the same if you leave words out.

questions.prompt: Correct the spelling: ‘responsability’.
questions.explanation: The word has an i after the b: responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly and best embeds the quotation?
options: Birling dismisses “community and all that nonsense” (Birling, Act 1) as if it were a joke.
Birling dismisses the idea of community, he treats it as a joke.
birling dismisses the idea of community as a joke.
Birling dismisses the idea of community. As if it were a joke.
questions.explanation: The quotation is embedded inside the sentence in quotation marks. The others contain a comma splice, a missing capital and a sentence fragment.

questions.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: Claiming standards you do not meet
A small model of something larger
questions.explanation: Precise vocabulary helps AO4 and makes analysis sharper.

questions.prompt: Correct this paragraph: ‘In an inspector calls, Priestly shows Mr Burling as a man who dosent care about his workers. Shiela and eric react diffrently to the inspector.’
questions.model: Model answer: In An Inspector Calls (underlined in handwriting), Priestley shows Mr Birling as a man who doesn’t care about his workers. Sheila and Eric react differently to the Inspector.
checklist: Capitalises and marks the title
Corrects Priestley and Birling
Corrects doesn’t, with its apostrophe
Corrects Sheila and capitalises Eric
Corrects differently and capitalises Inspector
questions.explanation: Names and key words are the easiest AO4 marks to secure.
